text: , "That the Bill be now read a Second time." –  .

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have three points of clarification to raise.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My first point is on the scope of platform services covered under the Bill.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: That said, the number of self-employed persons who use online matching platforms to provide other types of services is also growing.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: These services include domestic cleaning, beauty, therapeutic and caregiving services.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For example, when a domestic cleaning platform acquired a local cleaning company with 60 employees in 2021, it announced that it would be adding 1,000 more workers to its platform within one year.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: A chief executive officer (CEO) of a medical and caregiving platform service reported that between 2018 and 2021, the company observed a 10 times growth in demand for homecare, which would translate into a spike in the caregivers using its platform.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Given that the Bill already covers 90% of workers, can the Senior Minister of State share the rationale for not going further and covering all platform services?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Is there a principled difference between workers on delivery or ride-hail services platforms compared to platforms of other services?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Will the Ministry look into expanding the definition of "platform operators" and "platform workers" in the Bill to cover all types of platform services at a later date?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If so, does the Ministry have a timeline for reviewing the scope of the definition?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In light of the rising number of self-employed persons who use online matching platforms to provide other types of services, I urge the Government to extend the protections under this Bill to cover all types of platform services.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My second point is on remedies available for platform workers who encounter discrimination and unfair dismissal.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I welcome the announcement of platform work associations which will have legal mandate to represent platform workers to address issues like fairer payment terms.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: While this is a good step, it may not go far enough to protect platform workers from unfair dismissal or discrimination by the platform operators.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This Bill does not appear to prohibit platform operators from unfairly removing a platform worker from the platform service or making decisions which discriminate against the platform worker.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Food delivery riders have complained about being unfairly penalised, warned or suspended for food spillage or other customer complaints.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Private hire vehicle drivers have complained about wrongful forfeiture of incentives and wrongful removal from the platform.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The lack of a low-cost dispute resolution mechanism in the Bill, such as the equivalent of filing a claim at Tripartite Alliance for Dispute Management (TADM) or a mediation request at TAFEP, means that platform workers may have little or no viable options to dispute the platform operator's decision to remove or discriminate against the platform worker.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This would result in a loss of income to the platform worker and this will, in turn, affect their housing and retirement adequacy.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Senior Minister of State share whether the Ministry looked into the need for mechanisms for recourse against unfair dismissal and discrimination?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If so, what were the considerations for excluding these mechanisms from this Bill?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Will the Ministry study the possibility of including these mechanisms in the future?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My third and final point is on the transparency of decision-making by platform operators.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Regulators in other states have introduced policies to make more transparent decision-making by platform operators.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For platform workers, this could mean transparency over key factors, such as the distance, destination and share of tips received, how their rating was derived, which, in turn, affects the jobs assigned to them and the amount that they earn.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Senior Minister of State share if the Ministry looked into the necessity of introducing similar provisions under this Bill?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If so, can the Senior Minister of State share why these provisions were not included?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If such provisions were not studied, will the Ministry consider looking into provisions which require platform operators to improve the transparency of their decision-making systems and processes?

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: These are our taxi drivers, private-hire car drivers and delivery workers.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: They make up a significant population in our workforce.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Under the proposed Platform Workers Bill, platform workers will now gain rights and legal protection they did not enjoy before.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: On this Bill, I will speak on and raise clarifications around three key areas of the Bill, namely: one, the implications of Central Provident Fund (CPF); two, workplace injury compensation; and three, the scope of this Bill.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: CPF ensures that workers have a safety net to meet future needs.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: It encourages workers to start saving for a home at a younger age, sets aside a fund for healthcare and facilitates long-term financial planning for retirement.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Hopefully, this will alleviate the worries of workers about reduction in take-home pay and encourage more workers to opt in for CPF.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: While the introduction of CPF coverage for platform workers is promising and should be commended, there are potential downside risks that should be addressed.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: First, mandating CPF contributions may unintentionally frame platform work as a viable, long-term career path for younger workers.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: However, it is important to acknowledge that platform work rarely offers long-term development.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Unlike employees, platform workers do not have the same access to continuous learning or promotion opportunities.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: This limits their career progression, especially when they are often isolated from professional networks and not levelling up their skills over time.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Additionally, platform workers do not have the full benefits that employees enjoy.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Platform work is subject to market forces and can be an unstable source of income.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: It is preferably not a long-term career plan for all, especially for people in the early stages of their working life.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Yet, full-time platform workers who want to switch careers often find it difficult to leave this line of work.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: On one hand, platform workers may be willing to spend their time upskilling and applying for jobs.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: But that time could be spent completing gigs to make more money.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: It is a luxury to some platform workers, a luxury most cannot afford.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Contrast this with lower-wage employees in sectors under the Progressive Wage Model (PWM).

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: The PWM maps out a clear career pathway for wages to increase.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Employees are required to attend training to improve their productivity and skills.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Platform workers do not benefit from such structured support.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Unlike lower-wage employees, there is no incentive to improve their skills within their ecosystem.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Even if they do secure a job, it may be difficult for platform workers to get used to a more traditional working environment.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: After all, while platform work offers for more flexibility and autonomy, traditional employees are usually under direct supervision at the workplace.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Transitioning to this can be challenging and may discourage platform workers from seeking or staying in traditional employment.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: We therefore need to proactively support our platform workers, especially the younger ones, to find and remain in a stable job.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: The Government currently has a range of support measures catered to lower-wage workers and unemployed individuals.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: These include the Workfare Skills Support Scheme and the Career Conversion Programmes.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: More recently, during the National Day Rally, Prime Minister Lawrence Wong also announced the Jobseeker Support scheme, recognising the difficulties faced by the involuntarily unemployed.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Perhaps, we can introduce tailored programmes to address the opportunity cost that platform workers face.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Or could the Government calibrate existing schemes so that more are incentivised to prepare themselves for a long-term career.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: As these concerns have already been explored in detail by hon Members of the House yesterday, I will not be repeating them here.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Instead, I would like to ask three clarifying questions.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Second and related to this, will the Government consider regulating the assignment of jobs by platform operators?

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Such regulation could come in the form of clear guidelines to ensure that there is no discrimination against CPF-contributing workers.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: These guidelines could be developed jointly with platform work associations, platform operators and the Government.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Full transparency on how jobs are assigned will be key to ensuring fair and objective job allocation and maintaining the trust between platform operators and platform workers.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: And third, platform workers are rightly concerned that platform operators might react to the need to make CPF payments by increasing the commission collected from them or reducing their incentives and bonuses.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: The introduction of CPF may therefore risk further shrinking the take-home pay of workers in the long run. in light of this, it would be helpful if the Government can share how it envisions this playing out in the long-term and how this risk will be mitigated.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Moving on from CPF, the Bill also covers workplace injury compensation for platform workers.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Safety is a big concern for delivery riders, especially those who use bicycles or e-bikes.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Long hours, rushing to complete orders on time and harsh weather conditions put them at a heightened risk of accidents.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Similarly, ride-hail drivers face a higher risk of accidents than regular motorists, simply because they are on the road for longer.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: It is only right that we look after their safety and that we should be comprehensive in our approach.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Beyond addressing workplace injuries, we should also strive to support the overall health and well-being of platform workers to prevent serious injuries.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: This Bill does not provide platform workers with benefits common to employees, such as sick leave or annual leave.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: As touched upon earlier, platform workers, especially younger ones, aged 30 and below, for whom CPF contributions will become compulsory, may worry about their reduced take-home pay.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: To compensate, they might work longer hours which, by the way, also limits significantly any time for exercise.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: After taking time off to recover, they may feel pressured to work even harder to make up for lost time, further adding stress and harming their physical and mental well-being.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Over time, this creates a vicious cycle of overwork and exhaustion.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: The issue of annual leave and medical benefits for platform workers has been brought up by other hon Members of Parliament (MPs) in the past.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: I note that Senior Minister of State Koh has shared the reasons for excluding these other benefits in his opening speech yesterday.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: I certainly understand the need to strike a fine balance.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: I hope that the Government can carefully consider the inclusion of these benefits in future iterations of the Act or study specific measures to address this gap so that we take better care of platform workers.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Platform workers may have to deal with unreasonable behaviour from platform users.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: For instance, if a restaurant takes too long to prepare food, the delivery rider may be unfairly blamed for the delay and receive lower ratings.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Miscommunications between ride-hail drivers and passengers may also occur, such as when the pick-up point is in an unfamiliar spot or is difficult to locate.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: These frustrations may result in disagreements, which have the potential to escalate.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Ride-hail drivers have to maintain a minimum overall rating to keep their account and be eligible for incentives and bonuses.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: It makes them less likely to retaliate or defend themselves when facing verbal abuse, for fear of poor reviews or complaints.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Women drivers are also vulnerable to sexual harassment from passengers.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: In comparison, some workers in other industries have protections in place.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Security officers, for example, are protected from assault and harassment under the Private Security Industry Act.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Such protections being legislated sends a strong signal that harassment will not be tolerated.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Given that harassment is a real risk in platform work, will the Government consider including protections from harassment in a future iteration of the Act?

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Platform workers deserve to feel safe and have sufficient recourse in the event of harassment.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: In the healthcare sector, the Tripartite Framework for the Prevention of Abuse and Harassment in Healthcare was launched last December.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: The framework sets out, I quote, "a standardised, zero-tolerance policy against all forms of abuse and harassment towards healthcare workers".

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: If not through legislation, I hope that the Government could at least consider modifying and applying such a framework to platform workers too.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: In doing so, platform operators and platform work associations can collaborate to improve reporting and prevent situations that lead to abuse and harassment.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: I am heartened to know that platform workers will be supported in their retirement planning and in having workplace injury compensation.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Under the proposed Bill, "platform service" means a service specified in the First Schedule that is provided through a platform, digital or otherwise, by a platform operator exercising management control in respect of the provision of that service by platform workers.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: There are other platform workers who need to be safeguarded.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: As an example, I would like to call particular attention to locum nurses, especially those who find work through caregiving platforms.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: They help plug the gap of providing home nursing services, especially with our ageing population.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: All providers of caregiving services deserve to be recognised; so do other platform workers who provide services that keep us all going.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: They should be entitled to having their rights, protections and representation provided for.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: If the Government is considering expanding the scope of the Act in future to provide for more platform workers, it would be helpful to understand the timeline for such amendments.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We have heard throughout this debate stories and statistics about the vulnerabilities platform workers face.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: This Bill seeks to address those vulnerabilities, providing platform workers with baseline protections and hope for a more secure future.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: This debate is close to my heart because there are many platform workers living in my constituency, Woodlands.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Indeed, when COVID-19 struck, our community centres (CCs) in Woodlands had the longest lines for Temporary Relief Fund grants in the whole country.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: In truth, there is no one face of a platform worker.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Our platform workers are a very diverse group with different situations and needs.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Some turned to platform work after many failed attempts to land another job.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Some turned to platform work to have the flexibility to manage their own time, to accommodate caregiving responsibilities, or simply to have more time with their families.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: For others, platform work is a side gig to a full-time job to boost their incomes.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We have students, working part-time to supplement their family incomes, to pay for school or for additional pocket money.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We have those who struggle to make a decent income, living day-to-day on whatever income they make on any given day.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We have heard several times of how for many platform workers, their expenses exceed their income.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But we also have what I call the "chiongsters", who have mastered exactly where and when they should be active on which platform to generate the most income.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The two-wheeler segment is very different from the four-wheeler segment and the no-vehicle segment, and within the two-wheeler segment, the motorbike segment is different from the bicycle segment.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: So, we must consider all these differences in designing and implementing these reforms.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But I hope we can all agree on two basic tenets.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: First, platform work should remain part of the landscape.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It offers opportunities for thousands of Singaporeans who need or prefer to have the flexibility of setting their own schedules.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: As an industry, the platform economy must remain sustainable even if there may be some failures or consolidations among the operators.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Second, all workers, employee or self-employed, high-income or low-income, should be treated fairly and with dignity and should have basic protections and a secure future.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: All workers should be treated fairly and with dignity.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The question before us therefore is not just how to protect these workers, but how to balance their need for flexibility with the need for fairness, security and dignity.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: These measures are not about taking away flexibility but about ensuring that in their pursuit of a livelihood, platform workers are not left without a safety net, because flexibility should not mean insecurity.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Similarly, a balanced approach will need to be adopted in the proposed safety codes so that they protect the safety and health of platform workers without taking away the flexibility and autonomy that some platform workers want, considering their own personal situations, for example, on scheduling and work hours, or stifling innovation on the part of the platform operators even while they meet the new regulatory requirements.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It may be expedient to place the burden on one party – specifically, for the platform operators to absorb all the costs.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But a quick look at the numbers in the public domain suggest this could be untenable.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: One ride-hailing platform operator, for example, charges 10% commission on trip fares.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: That means their revenues are 10% of the fares.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Then, there are the WICA payments, plus the cost of compliance for all the new regulations.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Is there enough left for this to be sustainable for the platform operator to bear all these costs?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: So, yes, there will be costs and yes, some of these costs may indeed likely to be passed on.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But let us not forget that we as a society benefit from the services these workers provide.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It is only fair that the responsibility of ensuring their protection is shared among all stakeholders – the Government, platform operators and consumers.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: This will not be an easy balance, but this Government has shown that it will not shy away from doing the right thing.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: In this case, doing the right thing is making sure that our platform operators, who do so much for us, are not left behind without a safety net.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The Bill also provides a legal framework for platform work associations to represent platform workers.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: With the enactment of new laws, the platform work associations will play an important role in representing platform workers on these new laws and more broadly, giving platform workers a voice.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: In considering the scope for what the platform work associations will intervene in, the associations should take a comprehensive approach, going beyond focusing on the new benefits, health and safety standards as well as prices and incentives schemes to address other things that impact platform workers' rights, well-being and long-term sustainability, including support in improving working conditions, resolving disputes with platform operators and customers, including abuse and harassment, training and career development, and promoting respect, dignity and societal recognition for the contributions of platform workers to society.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: On speaking up for workers in their grievances, food delivery riders in Woodlands told me of a particular customer in Woodlands who frequently buys alcohol on the weekends.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Every single time, he will report spillage or breakages, resulting in penalties for many, many delivery riders.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Yet, the platform has ignored their complaints and they feel there is no way for them to fight back.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Other delivery riders have told me about orders that are too heavy for one rider or stacked orders that force them to go in opposite directions and are impossible to complete within the time limit while private hire drivers have told me about how the cleaning fee given to them for cleaning their vehicles when a passenger throws up in the car barely goes to cover the actual cost of cleaning, let alone the loss of income for the period during which the driver cannot take on passengers while airing the car to eliminate odours.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: These may sound like small things to us, but these small things add up and have a real impact on the lived experiences of platform workers and their feelings of fairness, respect and dignity.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Platform work associations have a role to play in effecting positive changes in their lives.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: What is probably more important is how we are going to go about implementing the provisions in a way that is inclusive for all stakeholders, engenders trust and advances long-term benefits for society as well as for the platform workers.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: To that end, I have a few questions for the Senior Minister of State.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Will it be standardised across all platform operators?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Will consideration be given for minimising the burden on the platform worker while balancing efficiency?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: For example, will the platform operators withhold the maximum rate for everyone even if the platform worker consistently earns below the income thresholds for the maximum rate?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: How will it take into account the different risk profiles of different platform worker segments?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: What will be the monitoring and enforcement mechanisms to ensure that platform companies are full complying with new workplace safety and health codes and workplace injury compensation regulations?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: At the same time, how do we avoid a system of spurious claims?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: What is the scope of representation that will be undertaken by the platform work associations?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Will the Government provide financial literacy programmes or advisory services to help platform workers understand the long-term benefits of CPF contributions and plan for their retirement?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: How can we ensure that Singapore remains a hub for innovation in the platform economy?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: How can the Government encourage platform companies to invest in technology to make platform work safer and more efficient and to develop new services that bring more value to the economy and can help to offset any share of the costs of this Bill that they may incur?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: How can the Government explore how technology can help platform workers to better track their working hours, manage their CFP contributions and access support services.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: How will the Government ensure that these reforms genuinely improve the lives of platform workers without unintended consequences?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: What are the longer-term metrics, for example, for home ownership?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Like those from other races, some become platform workers because they could not find another job, or another job that will pay them more.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But many become platform workers, and remain platform workers, because they value the flexibility that the job allows for them to spend more time with their families, or to fulfil caregiving responsibilities for their children or aged parents.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: A common issue among platform workers is that they have very little CPF.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I often hear people say that they prefer to manage their own money and save on this own, that they don’t want their money locked away.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Some say that they don’t make enough to set aside money in CPF.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: For older workers who have paid off their housing loans, or workers who have spouses or other family members who have CPF, it is perhaps not such an issue.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But for others, especially the younger workers looking to start or grow their families, they cannot leverage on CPF to buy a flat or to hold on a flat.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I met a resident in a desperate financial situation.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Her husband, who was the sole breadwinner as a food delivery rider had recently passed away from illness, and she was on the verge of losing the HDB flat she lived in with her four young children.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The arrears had started accumulating when he fell sick.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Her late husband could not work and his medical treatments drained their savings as he had no insurance.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: In this one example, you see all the vulnerabilities of being a platform worker, with no protections for healthcare, housing or insurance.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: This should not be the case, and we should all support this Bill that gives platform workers these basic protections.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Thus, it is important to improve understanding of the long term benefits of CPF and how it works, among platform workers in our community.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Like Woodlands resident Mr K, in his 50s.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: He became a food delivery rider after he suffered a stroke.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: While he recovered from his stroke, he and his employer mutually agreed that it was best he leave the company.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: For him, food delivery has given him a lifeline to continue to earn a living, where he could work when he felt up to it and stop when he couldn’t.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It’s for my future he said, if I cannot work anymore, or if anything happens to me again.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Part of his CPF goes to paying for Medishield.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I asked Mr K: will you like your son to work in the gig economy?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And this is what we must never stop striving for.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: More opportunities, more options, for workers, especially the young, in our community, who have a long career ahead of them.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Even while we provide much needed protection and security for the platform workers of today, we must ensure that we do not stop providing opportunities for all workers to gain new relevant skills in the fast changing economy of tomorrow.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We must also ensure that we must press on in providing more flexible work arrangements within traditional employment, that can better accommodate family and caregiving needs, so the gig economy is not the only option for flexibility.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It is and must remain an option, but not the only option.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: So, we must continue to revisit our labour policies and processes from time to time.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We must continue to improve financial literacy in our community.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We must make sure that our policy making is inclusive and the voices of our community are represented. : In conclusion, Mr Speaker, as we move forward together and forge our new social compact, we must not lose sight of the values that define us as a nation: fairness, justice and care for one another.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Platform workers deserve the same dignity, respect, protections as any other worker, and this Bill is an important step in ensuring that.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Let us not only support the livelihoods of our gig workers but also secure their futures.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: For the delivery rider who rides through the rain to bring you your dinner, for the private hire vehicle driver who works late into the night to support his family, this Bill is about giving them the security they need without taking away the flexibility they value.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: This Bill rightfully acknowledges the crucial role platform workers play and seeks to address some of the issues they face.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: It is worth emphasising the significance of their role in Singapore's economy.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: During the pandemic lockdown, they became essential to our daily lives, ensuring the continuity of services and even boosting Singapore's productivity.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: When the circuit breaker was in place, our food delivery riders and companies were at the forefront, delivering tens of thousands of food orders all over Singapore, especially for those who were in quarantine.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Not only did these workers alleviate the difficulty of individuals in quarantine, these unsung heroes also ensured that food and beverage (F&B) businesses stayed afloat, by continuing with their takeaway businesses.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: It signals a positive shift, one that recognises not just their contributions but their rightful place within our economic framework.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: In my view, this new legislation also benefits employers.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: For businesses and business owners, this Bill can lead to better relationships between businesses and their platform workers, as the regulations provide clearer guidelines on rights and responsibilities.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: This could result in higher worker satisfaction and loyalty.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: By formalising the rights and obligations of platform workers and operators, the Bill reduces legal ambiguities.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Businesses can operate with more confidence, knowing they comply with regulations, which can help avoid potential legal disputes.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Furthermore, businesses which comply with the new regulations might gain a better reputation among consumers and workers, who value fair treatment and worker protection.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: This could attract more customers and better performing workers to the respective platforms.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: The regulation of platform operators also ensures a level playing field, preventing unfair practices and promoting healthy competition within the digital economy.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: This will stimulate innovation and improve efficiency among platform service providers.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: This Bill also can lead to the development of new business models and services within the gig economy, contributing to the diversification of Singapore's economy.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: This could lead to higher costs for consumers and will reduce margins for businesses, potentially impacting the competitiveness of Singapore-based platforms.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: One, will there be any Government support measures and assistance to help these businesses?

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Two, does this Bill apply to all types of platform services, including those that are emerging or certainly are less common?

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Three, are there any exemptions for certain types of platforms or services and, if so, what are the criteria for these exemptions?

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Four, how will the Bill affect existing contracts between platform operators and workers?

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Will there be a transition period for compliance?

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Five, what happens if a current platform work agreement conflicts with the provisions of the Bill?

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: I recognise that effective implementation and enforcement of the Bill’s provisions may require significant additional resources to ensure that all platform operators comply with the regulations.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Six, how does the Ministry hope to ensure the seamless execution of these new regulations?

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: These figures reflect a return to pre-pandemic 2019 levels, suggesting that we may be observing a steady-state situation for platform work in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: However, despite this decline, platform operators and workers continue to have a disproportionately large impact on both our economy and society.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: The services they provide remain essential to many aspects of daily life and it is in this context that the Platform Workers Bill takes on heightened significance.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: The merit of this Bill lies in its balance.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: It alleviates cost pressures on our platform operators which might otherwise lead to reduced job opportunities or, in a worse case, business closures.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: At the same time, it ensures that our platform workers receive basic employment protections, such as income security and workplace safety. : The Bill, however, adopts an exclusive definition of platform services currently limited to delivery and ride-hailing services.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: As such, I would like to raise an essential clarification.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: The evolution of the platform economy means that new types of services will inevitably emerge.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: It is essential that we anticipate this by ensuring the flexibility of the Bill to respond to future developments.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: The second point I wish to address concerns the requirements placed on platform operators to provide work injury compensation insurance and ensure that platform workers require adequate training.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: These are crucial protections, but platform workers often provide their services across multiple operators, which raises a key question.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Is there a national mechanism that coordinates insurance coverage and training across operators?

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Without such coordination, we risk unnecessary duplication of costs which will likely be passed on to both platform operators and, eventually, consumers.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: A centralised or coordinated approach could help streamline these processes, reducing costs for all stakeholders while ensuring that platform workers are adequately protected.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: I now turn to the potential impact of the Platform Workers Bill on our broader workforce.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: The Bill has the potential to level the playing field between platform operators and traditional employers by ensuring that platform workers receive equitable protections and CPF contributions.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: This will support their housing and retirement adequacy.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: While the impact on employment preferences may be varied, some platform workers might choose to transition back to more traditional employment sectors for better long-term career prospects.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: To facilitate this transition, can the Government consider expanding the scope of existing programmes like WSG's Career Conversion Programmes (CCPs) as well as the Mid-Career Pathways Programmes administered by the Singapore Business Federation to create an accelerated, effective pathway for platform workers seeking new opportunities in traditional sectors and supporting their career transition?

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Currently, these programmes already offer structured training, salary support and job placement assistance, which could be adapted to the needs of platform workers looking to reskill and move back into traditional roles.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Can we help our platform workers transition more efficiently by pre-identifying CCPs that platform workers can tap into since there are over 100 CCPs available today?

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: These could be focused on adjacent roles, such as transport and logistics, or even retail and F&B, which can offer opportunities for those seeking new career options.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Importantly, can these programmes be tailored to more workplace-based training and less classroom-based training?

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: This hands-on training element will help ramp up the onboarding process and ensure a fast and efficient transition into new roles and helping close the manpower gaps that some sectors are currently experiencing.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: The additional costs imposed on platform operators, such as the requirements for insurance and CPF contributions, will inevitably lead to higher service costs.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: This is particularly concerning for smaller businesses, which may already be operating on tight margins and lack the resources to absorb such costs internally.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: The increased costs resulting from the Bill are likely to affect SMEs more acutely, as they often rely on platform services due to their limited ability to manage their functions inhouse.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Additionally, can the Government collaborate with trade associations and businesses to explore comprehensive support mechanisms, such as subsidies, tax relief or any other measures to help alleviate cost pressures and maintain the competitiveness of SMEs in this challenging landscape?

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: At the same time, will enhanced measures be put in place to ensure that businesses do not resort to unnecessary price hikes, thus protecting consumers from unjustified cost transfers while maintaining fair pricing practices?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: I do, nonetheless, have some questions for the Senior Minister of State on the scope of the Bill and on potential future developments.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: As the Association of Women for Action and Research, or AWARE, has pointed out in its response to the public consultation on this Bill, the Bill excludes other types of services that are delivered via online platforms.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Some examples of these include beauty and grooming services, caregiving services and house cleaning services.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: These types of platform services will not fall within the definition set out in the First Schedule of the proposed Bill.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Platform workers in the delivery and ride-hailing sectors tend to be male, whereas a greater proportion of workers in the areas of beauty, grooming, caregiving and cleaning services tend to be female.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: So, if we consider the framing of the Bill from this perspective, it appears that a good number of female platform workers may not actually be able to benefit from the protections offered by this new law.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: So, my first clarification for the Senior Minister of State is why these types of platform workers have been excluded from the scope of the Bill?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: I would also like to ask if there are future plans to include a wider range of platforms for the delivery of services within the ambit of this Bill.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: This is a point that has been raised by a number of Members, and I join them, too, in raising my concerns.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: My second clarification has to do with the term “human intervention on a regular or routine basis,” as set out in clause 6 of the Bill.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: My next set of questions has to do with gender and other imbalances in the gig economy, especially where digital platforms are concerned.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: AWARE’s submission, which I referred to earlier, makes important points about the functionality of platform services which the present Bill does not seem to overtly address.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Ride-hail platforms, for example, generally prioritise job assignments based on driver ratings.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: This is something that is determined by both the platform’s algorithms and by client reviews.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: The theory here is that workers will be incentivised to provide good service so as not to achieve poor ratings.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: On the flip side of things, platform workers may not themselves be adequately protected from harassment and discrimination if unfair complaints are made by malicious customers.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: The hope, presumably, is that these kinds of grievances can be taken up by platform work associations, which are provided for in Part 3 of the Bill.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: I seek the Government’s confirmation that this an area that platform work associations will be actively looking into.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: The next point I would like to make is that while we may assume that platforms are gender-blind and merely match customers and workers in the most efficient way, the design of these platforms can inadvertently result in gender imbalances being perpetuated.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: To put it another way, digital labour platforms are built using real-world data, but we must not forget that the real world is itself full of biases and imbalances.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: For example, if workers have unpredictable caregiving responsibilities and need to suddenly cancel their work assignments because of these responsibilities, they may accordingly be penalised by platforms which operate by automatically allocating tasks to workers.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Similarly, if ride-hail or delivery workers choose to decline jobs that take place late at night or in areas where they feel it is unsafe to work, they will lose out on potential job opportunities.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Algorithms, of course, are built in such a way that where there is less supply, the prices charged to consumers are much higher.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: So, there is an opportunity to earn more if you take on work that other people either do not want to do or cannot do.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: This leads to a situation where workers who are either willing to put themselves at risk or who perhaps feel that they can handle these risks better, well, they have the potential to earn more than others who do not.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Given that women still tend to take on the lion’s share of caregiving responsibilities in society and given that women are also a group who may be exposed to higher levels of risks when working alone in remote areas or late into the night, the overall outcome is then a situation where gender pay imbalances can continue to be perpetuated even in the realm of platform work.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: This is one possible solution but the more fundamental issue, to me, is in basically ensuring that platform workers are treated equitably and are not unfairly penalised for things like caregiving responsibilities and for prioritising their own safety.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: The Platform Workers Bill being debated today does not seem to address this specific point, but I hope that the Government will advocate for this when dealing with platform operators.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: The next point I would like to make is a broader one.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: While the Bill today addresses the problems faced by certain types of platform workers, let us not forget that there are other specific communities which are also made up of a large number of freelancers.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Again, it is a well-known fact that this is higher than the national average, which stands at less than one in five.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: In fact, in many research reports and articles, artists are often referred to as the “original gig economy workers.” Admittedly, platform workers are not exactly the same as arts freelancers, certainly in the way that they have been defined for the purposes of the Bill today, but the two groups do face similar stresses.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: This is all information and feedback that is well-known to the Government through its many engagement sessions over a number of years with the arts community.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: And there are examples that we can draw from in jurisdictions that have enacted specific laws to protect freelancers like this.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: In Illinois, also in the United States (US), the Freelance Worker Protection Act offers similar safeguards.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Closer to home, in Korea, the Artist Welfare Act seeks to protect artists’ job security and rights in areas, such as contractual arrangements and work injury compensation.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: So, while I welcome and support the Platform Workers Bill, I would also like to take the opportunity today to ask the Senior Minister of State if this important piece of legislation can be seen as a step towards providing better workplace conditions for a wider group of self-employed individuals and, in particular, those in the arts community?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: The usual argument that is applied here is that freelancers are expected to make sacrifices in exchange for flexibility, but these kinds of views are so much harder to sustain in a post-COVID world.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Now even workers in traditional employer-employee relationships seek more personal autonomy and flexible work arrangements.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: In Singapore, the rise of platform work has underscored the urgency of addressing new challenges in ensuring decent working conditions, fair wages, comprehensive social security coverage, and robust workers' rights.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: The rapid expansion of platform based work has necessitated a re-evaluation of our existing framework to safeguard the interests of these workers who are increasingly becoming important in our economy.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: These moves represent a significant milestone, emerging from years of advocacy and collaborative efforts with the Labour Movement and the tripartite partners, to address key issues and develop a mutually agreeable approach to platform work in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: While this legislative step is indeed a positive advancement, it is important to recognise that there is still room for further improvement.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Platform workers, particularly those in lower-income brackets, face unique challenges in securing their financial future.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: The Labour Movement has consistently advocated for measures that protect their interests, ensuring that they receive fair treatment and support in navigating these changes.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: The CPF Transition Support Scheme reflects the responsiveness of MOM and the CPF Board (CPFB) to the feedback provided by our Associations.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: This phased approach is particularly significant as it allows platform workers time to adapt to the new contribution structure while still securing the benefits that come with enhanced CPF contributions.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: The Labour Movement views this as a positive development that underscores the importance of collaborative dialogue between government bodies and worker representatives in shaping policies that are both fair and sustainable.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: This change, alongside the eventual alignment of CPF contribution rates between platform workers and employees, ensures that platform workers will receive the same level of WIS benefits as traditional employees, including higher WIS amounts and a larger proportion of the supplement in cash.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: These adjustments are particularly beneficial for low-wage workers, addressing both their immediate financial needs and long-term financial security.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: The transition to monthly WIS payments is a significant step for low-wage platform workers, who often face unpredictable income patterns due to the nature of gig work.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: By receiving WIS on a monthly basis, these workers will have a more consistent and reliable source of income, helping them to better manage their day-to-day expenses and financial planning.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: These enhancements not only provide immediate financial relief but also contribute to the workers’ long-term financial well-being by bolstering their CPF savings, which are essential for retirement.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Opting into CPF not only helps build a safety net for the future but also provides immediate benefits such as access to healthcare, housing, and other essential needs.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Given the importance of securing their financial future, it is essential that the government steps up its efforts to encourage platform workers in this age group (30 years old and above) to opt into CPF.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: The Government must recognise the unique challenges and concerns that platform workers face and ensure that the CPF system is viewed as a vital component of their financial planning.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: This requires a multi-faceted approach that includes comprehensive educational campaigns and targeted outreach programs to help platform workers understand the long-term benefits of CPF contributions.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: There is a genuine concern that these workers may be offered fewer job opportunities or lower earnings if they choose to participate fully in the CPF system.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: To mitigate these fears, the government should collaborate closely with platform operators to ensure that CPF participation does not lead to any form of disadvantage for workers.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: By implementing policies that protect platform workers from potential discrimination and by engaging in clear communication with both workers and operators, the government can create an environment, where opting into CPF is seen as the best choice.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: This will not only help platform workers secure a better financial future but also contribute to a more stable and equitable labour market.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: The time to act is now, and the government must lead the way in making CPF participation a priority for all platform workers.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Platform workers face constant pressure to work longer hours just to earn a living and this means that many platform workers find it challenging to invest time and resources in personal development and career growth.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: This lack of progression not only affects their current financial stability but also hampers their ability to transition into more sustainable and fulfilling careers.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: This includes providing targeted upskilling programs and career transition support.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: By offering vocational training and educational opportunities tailored to the needs of platform workers, the government can help them acquire new skills and qualifications that are in demand in other sectors.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Additionally, creating pathways for mentorship and career counselling can assist these workers in navigating the job market and identifying potential career opportunities.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Naseer, who left his job as an operations manager November last year.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Since then, he has struggled with unemployment and relied on ad hoc security gigs and occasional platform work to support his family.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Despite his efforts, the limited career progression in platform work made it difficult for him to build a stable future.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: However, with the support of the Greenlane initiative through Focus Area 4 under M3, Mr.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Naseer secured a new job in April this year as a customer operations manager and remains optimistic about his future.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: This story highlights the importance of targeted support programs that can help workers like him make the transition from platform work to more stable and rewarding careers.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Investing in these programs not only benefits the individuals directly but also contributes to a more resilient and dynamic workforce overall.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: To our platform workers: our Associations, such as the National Taxi Association (NTA), National Private Hire Vehicles Associations (NPHVA) and National Delivery Champions Association (NDCA), have been working hard to improve your welfare behind the scenes.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: We now have the power to speak up and take action to protect you.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: We can negotiate for fairer treatment by platforms.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: When you have grievances with platforms, we can step in to support you.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: We cannot do this on our own, but we can do it together.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Join us to make your voices count. : Mr Speaker, in conclusion, the Labour Movement warmly welcomes the recognition of the challenges faced by the platform workers through the implementation of initiatives, such as the PCTS and WIS Support scheme.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: These measures are a significant step forward in acknowledging and addressing the issues of employee protection within the gig economy.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: However, we must recognise that the more comprehensive efforts are needed to address the broader clarity face by platform workers.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: By doing so, we can help platform workers navigate the evolving job market and secure more stable and fulfilling careers.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Speaker, Sir, the Labour Movement, comprising unionists, association leaders and NTUC, have worked hard with the tripartite partners to bring this Bill to fruition.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Without tripartism and symbolic relationship with the People's Action Party (PAP), this will not be possible.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: We have seen examples of other countries, where the unions, companies and government cannot agree on the protection needed for platform workers.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: In the end, the platform workers are the ones who suffer.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Together, we can build a more equitable and resilient workforce, ensuring no one is left behind in the face of economic change.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: With NTUC and our associations, let us continue to listen to the voice of our platform workers to not only address the immediate challenges faced by the platform workers, but also pave the way from a brighter and more secure future for all.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: NTUC will continue to champion their interests because every platform worker matters.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: I believe, without exception, all of us have been acquainted personally with the ease of a platform service.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: With the click of a button, we have our food delivered to our doorstep.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: Another click books our trip to or from home.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: And yet another click could ensure a timely parcel delivery or a quick retrieval of important documents.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: The platform service is so efficient, straightforward and with an interface that is easy to use that often, we have come to rely on it as part of our daily lives.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: The service platform also allows us to get what we want, when we want it and how we want it.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: We also felt its special utility during the COVID-19 pandemic, to go "contactless" and that the delivery can be made without human contact or much further instruction.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: We specify the need, make the order and hey presto, it appears at our doorstep.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: We decide the destination and agree on the payment and the ride arrives and sends us to the destination with much fuss or kerfuffle.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: So easy it is to use a platform service that sometimes, we forget the human in the loop, which is why I feel this Bill and the Platform Workers Act is overdue.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: Platform workers often choose such gig jobs for flexibility of time but this need for flexibility also sometimes arises from a function of their harsh life circumstances and not necessarily by way of their preferred choice.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: It comes with challenges, including job insecurity, social isolation, irregular work hours and long days.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: Any injury or illness, a family emergency or unexpected vehicular breakdown can have a very direct impact on our platform workers and without the same sense of safety net and security salaried workers have and are protected for.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: Because in platform work it is suggested that the more you work the more you earn, it is also tempting to work more and more such that the platform worker, at least, in the moment, may consider disregarding his own safety, health and welfare to make that delivery or service count and bring that additional dollar back home.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: Add that to the contactless nature of how platform services work, that a delivery that can almost feel automatic and be bereft of any human interaction, the lack of collective bargaining power that platform workers have to put their welfare first in this line of work and an imbalance of power and control between platform companies and workers, it really puts us on the path of potentially dehumanising our platform workers if we leave things be as they are.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: To that end, I thank the MOM for looking into this very important area for platform workers alongside the unions, employers and other tripartite partners.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: Many of them work hard and are often drenched in perspiration just to earn a living, sometimes disregarding the risks to their own health and safety.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: When a platform service relies on an algorithm without any direct human involvement; when there is lesser human interaction, either between the service users, the platform workers or the platform operators; and when a service can be accepted or fulfilled in a contactless way or without human contact; we can easily forget about having compassion for the platform workers behind these services.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: This is key in enhancing the well-being of the platform workers, especially for the lower income group.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: It further reinforces the emphasis and responsibility of platform operators so that they show more concern towards the needs of this sector, in terms of the workers’ rights, employment, safety and health issues.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: This Bill also specifically focuses on addressing concerns and dealing with their long-term insecurities as platform workers, so that it is equal to and aligned with workers in other industries.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: I hope this the first of many concrete measures for our platform workers to raise awareness on the importance of platform workers in our economy, thus showing our appreciation for the hard work and determination they show every day to earn a living.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: It is a very important step to provide justice and equality to our platform workers. : Mr Speaker, before I end, I have two clarifications for the purposes of this Bill.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: These could include household cleaning services, counselling, psychology and caregiving services, or even possibly overlap with certain professional services, such as home nursing and medical services, some already available through mobile applications.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: These platform services allow for ready provision of such services, have a platform operator already exercising management control of the particular service and also engage workers or professionals providing that service.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: This is because such workers or professionals, like their delivery and ride-hailing services counterparts, may opt for a flexible work arrangement, not wish to be tied to a traditional brick-and-mortar employer or institution and may well fall under the remit of a platform worker as we define it in this Bill today.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: Second, Mr Speaker, there would be some anxiety of workers, employers and users alike regarding the eventual implementation of Act.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: The costs of business will likely increase and ensuring their platforms and systems transit to the new model of engagement with their workers will require some time and effort.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: In this regard, I hope the Ministry can assure members, platform workers, employers and the public on the forward steps to be taken to ameliorate these concerns such that the transition to effecting this Bill, which I believe remains an important pillar for our platform workers, is done smoothly.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast): Mr Speaker, Sir, I rise in support of the Platform Worker Bills.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: First, I wish to declare my interest as the CEO of Strides Premier, a company that hires out limousines, private hire cars and taxis.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: New technology has created new jobs and platform work is one of them.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: However, many platform operators in Singapore are still struggling financially.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: These figures highlight the uncertainties faced by platform workers, who have little control over their financial security.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I am heartened to see that sections 16 to 18 of the Bill prioritise payments to platform workers over most other debts if a platform operator goes bankrupt.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Without this protection, many workers would be left vulnerable and unable to recover what is rightfully theirs.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The most notable part of the Bill is Part 3, which paves the way for the formation of platform work associations.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: NTUC has already announced its intention to register a new platform work association with MOM, which will formally represent platform workers and dissolve the National Private Hire Vehicles Association, National Delivery Champions Association and the National Taxi Association, which has the longest history.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: These new associations will give platform workers a voice, a place where their concerns are heard and their needs are addressed.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: This is a significant milestone for a group that has often felt unheard and they can now be more appropriately represented by the new platform work associations.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I recall knowing one particular taxi driver who used to deliver for GrabFood.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: For some reasons, he was banned from the GrabFood platform.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: When he switched to becoming a taxi driver, he found himself banned from GrabCar and GrabTaxi platforms as well, even though these services were not directly linked to GrabFood platform.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: In this case, I had to appeal on his behalf.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: With the new platform work associations, platform workers like him will have someone to turn to.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Platform workers will be better protected, no longer left to fend for themselves.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: If the Platform Worker Bill is passed, platform workers will also be required to contribute to their CPF accounts.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: While this may mean a slight drop in their take-home pay, it ultimately secures their future with higher overall earnings from the CPF contributions to the platform operators.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I also commend the move to keep CPF contribution rates consistent for platform workers below 65 from 2025 to 2027 as mandated in the Fourth Schedule.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: This is a positive departure from the current practice, where employers contribute less for those aged 55 to 65 compared to younger workers.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Many of us, especially those in this House, agree that the 60s today are the new 50s.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: People are healthier, active and can contribute just as much as their younger counterparts.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: This is one of the reasons why MOM is raising the retirement age.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I urge MOM to consider raising the employer's CPF contribution rates for all Singaporean employees aged 55 to 65 to match those below 55, aligning with the standards MOM imposed on platform operators.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: There was once an argument that older workers between 55 and 65 were less productive, making them less attractive hires.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: However, with the tight labour market and no significant drop in the productivity for this age group, most employers no longer consider lower CPF contribution rates for the older workers as a critical factor in hiring decisions.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I urge MOM to stand firm in protecting our older workers by raising their employer's CPF contribution rates, ensuring that they receive the same respect and support as their younger colleagues.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Perhaps, the Government Service, being the largest employer in Singapore, can take the lead.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Currently, they are paid based on their productivity.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Whether it is a 30-year-old or a 65-year-old private hire driver, their job is to safely transport passengers from point A to point B.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Similarly, whether food is delivered by a younger platform worker or an older one, the service remains the same.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Age should not dictate the value of their work.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: So, why should platform operators contribute less to older platform workers' CPF after 2027 when their productivity per job basis remains unchanged?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I urge MOM to consider maintaining the platform operator's CPF contribution rate for platform workers below 65, even beyond 2027.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: For those above 65, some may argue that they are more prone to workplace injuries, potentially leading to higher insurance costs.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: In such cases, a slightly lower CPF contribution rate might be justified, but we should always strive to balance fairness with practicality.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: To safeguard platform workers' housing and retirement needs, those under 30 will need to contribute to their CPF while platform operators must also make employer's CPF contributions for platform workers.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: However, the cost will ultimately be borne by someone.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Will platform operators transfer this increased cost to consumers?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: In other words, will private hire car fares increase?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Will food delivery fees be raised as a result?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: These are important issues we must pay attention to.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Especially in Singapore, most platform operators are still operating at a loss and are struggling to become profitable.

speaker: Mr Speaker
