speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: In fact, he has repeatedly used the words "independent" and "non-partisan".

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: The unions must be independent and non-partisan to be effective, that to represent our workers without fear and favour, unions have to be independent and non-partisan.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: And that they would, then, be in a better place to represent their workers and to negotiate.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Then, he also went on to say that to be able to better advocate for workers they need to— he said said that unions are trying their best to advocate for workers, but they face restrictions to do so because of the Government and legislation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: So, I would like to ask Mr Gerald Giam whether he has personal experience or data points or even anecdotes to suggest that actually, today, the symbiotic relationship between the PAP and NTUC has caused our unions or union leaders to face restrictions or not to be able to speak up without fear of favour.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Because I would like to suggest that yesterday, after your speech, I received so much feedback from many of our union leaders.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: That is because whatever you said does not represent their experience on the ground.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: So, I will make two points in response to what you have just said.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: So, that is a very important point I need to make known to you.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: And in fact, one of the union leaders wrote to me quickly to ask, where does Member Gerald Giam feel that there are any restrictions for the union leader to speak up.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: So, I think that is the question that I hope Mr Gerald Giam can address.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Maybe I can also highlight one of the posts by the Building Construction And Timber Industries Employees' Union, or BATU – so, do not just hear from me.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: It talked about the labour MPs and the relationship in the union, it said "the privilege of working closely with PAP MPs and Cabinet Ministers over the years as council advisers is apparent.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Their involvement has been instrumental in helping us advocate for policies that address the needs of workers and improve their livelihoods.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: This collaboration has allowed us to shape practical solutions for the challenges faced in our industries." So, the whole idea of this symbiotic relationship is not to control the unions, but rather, we want to be able to serve, to listen, to be close to the ground so that we can better support and better speak up for the workers and better represent our workers in Parliament or even outside.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: The second point I want to address is about independence and being non-partisan.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: One of the union leaders, who is also in the central committee, wrote this passionately in his post after hearing the Member's speech.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: He said this, let me quote, "I am heartened by the impassioned response from Brother Heng Chee How.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: On numerous occasions, I have discussed concerns of teachers without fear or favour with the STU advisors." And that is from Mike Thiruman from the Singapore Teachers' Union, or STU.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: They choose to be affiliated to the NTUC and to the PAP because of the results we have delivered, because of the outcomes we have delivered for workers and for many years, because "Every Worker Matters".

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: But what I am talking about is not so much that the unionists are not speaking up.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: What I am saying is that there are institutional constraints on them that prevent them from being able to really push forward a lot of the policies.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: Because if in the current set-up where the unions are, what I feel, subordinate to the PAP, the unions will only be able to push through their policies if their policies align with the PAP's priorities.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: They will not be able to override what the PAP wants to do.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: And can I ask the Senior Minister of State whether he can cite any instance where the NTUC has taken a public position that is contrary to the Government policy in recent times?

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: I asked the hon Member about his personal experience and data, and he has not been able to cite those.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: So, whatever he claims, he might have read it in other countries.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: I am not denying that that is your opinion and that is your view.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: But I would like to suggest that we do not make those assumptions for Singapore, because of what other people are practising or because of what you read as a theory of how unions can work with the ruling party.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: Our colleagues have mentioned yesterday that is not uncommon that unions across the world are aligned to political parties.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: We have gone through the years and worked very hard to make sure that we build this symbiotic relationship as a strong foundation built on trust.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: And we are not about to give it up just because the Member has some theoretical framework and he suggests that it is better for unions to be independent of the ruling party.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: Member Patrick Tay has been raising it for 14 years.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: The Government did not agree at the start, but finally, they did.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: Maybe the Member imagines that these policies come from the labour MPs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: But no, let me assure the Member that these policies, ideas and suggestions came from the workers and the union leaders because they best represent their workers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: And our job as labour MPs is to represent them.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: Sometimes, the Government will listen to us and implement immediately.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: And that is to guard against what we call "yellow unions", unions that might be acting on behalf of employers to the detriment of employees, and also we to ensure the officers in the union were not convicted for criminal breaches of trust because these are necessary to maintain the trust.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: I listened to the Member's roundabout defence of why unions need to be independent and all, and the WP will or will not seek relationship – I am very confused.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Does WP want to build relationship with unions or not?

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, is the Member saying that his relationship with the unions is a transactional one, not built on mutual win-win and a symbolic relationship?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: We are calling for a third way, which is independent unions with tripartite dialogue, to work towards achieving win-win outcomes for both workers and employers.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: So, it is this approach that we are trying to take.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: We are not trying to say that we do not work with unions at all or we are in full relationship and symbiosis with unions.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Because I am very confused on why the WP is called "Workers' Party", if they are not really so pro-unions to begin with.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: In their website, I was just reading from here, the website says, "Marshall announces the idea of forming a party for workers while addressing the delegates of the army, civil service unions at a conference and he said, 'We can evolve a plan where we can create a political party whose membership is exclusively confined to members of trade unions'." So, the history of the WP is to be a party for trade unions.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: How can you not be in a relationship that is closely intertwined when you want to be a party for trade unions?

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: I do not understand where you start from.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The only reason I do so is because he made a remark in his concluding address on WP leadership.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I second what my colleague, Mr Gerald Giam, has said but let me just state some points very clearly.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Two, on the Senior Minister of State's historical analysis of the WP, I think it disregards an important fact that more than 60 years have elapsed, and the political situation has changed dramatically and significantly.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This is not just true for the WP, it is also true for the PAP.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But since the Senior Minister of State is on history, let me refer to evidence of what I believe my colleague, Mr Gerald Giam, was thinking about when he was talking about an independent NTUC, through the eyes of history.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I am referring to a publication of NTUC, titled "50 years of the Labour Movement in Singapore", October 1966, "NTUC's cooperation: Not one way traffic": "At an NTUC delegates conference, Ho See Beng, now Secretary-General, reminded the Government and employers that the NTUC's cooperation in the task of economic development was not a one-way traffic.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: He took issue with the with Government leaders, particularly the Prime Minister, for speaking unendingly of labour's obligations while hardly touching on labour's rights and major grievances." I would be grateful if the Senior Minister of State can raise a single example of where an NTUC Secretary-General or a deputy secretary-general has spoken out against a 3G or 4G leader to defend the rights of workers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I am not suggesting that this is the gold standard or the test.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But this comes to the heart of what people see and believe to be a conflict of interest.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And when NTUC delegates are saying "Majulah PAP", I think people are entitled to question, "Do you speak for the party first or do you speak for workers first?"   So, it is a simple point.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The point is not about moving Singapore in a direction where employers, employees, workers, Government fight each other to the detriment of our society and our economic growth.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And I think we have been waylaid down that rabbit hole and we have got to just come back to the central point that was being made by Mr Gerald Giam.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Party interests cannot be more important than the interest of our workers and a symbiotic relationship does not mean that the NTUC is neutered or cannot openly speak out in the interest of workers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And I think Minister of State Desmond Tan has shared where the NTUC has spoken out, and I have no reason to believe that NTUC rank and file workers did not speak out.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: That is something I have to say, because I know some of them and I have to say I have to thank them for their service for our workers.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, just because the WP lost the relationship with worker unions long ago does not mean that because we can preserve relationship for 60 years that there is something wrong with the symbiotic relationship.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I am not going to respond to that point, but just to say that there is no question of losing a relationship in any way.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Again, I am happy to stand corrected if I misheard.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: But having had deep conversations with our platform operators and the platform workers themselves, the desire on both sides is to make sure that administrative costs are reduced, the burden is reduced and choice is given to the workers.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, from a theoretical perspective, the Member may be right – put them in and then those who want to get out, can apply to get out.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: But the operators who have to bear onboarding costs, these are real costs.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: To put everybody on the system in the beginning will require system enhancements, put everybody in and making sure that everyone is onboarded and then subsequently, if a majority or a large number, or whichever number it may be, chooses to opt out, there will be an additional cost to process those people who want to get out.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Just a quick point about the theoretical nature of the system, I would just emphasise that this is not theoretical at all.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Systems around the world, public policy systems, including what I have just cited – CPF LIFE – along with the UK's Nudge Unit have already used opt-out systems as a default, as a mechanism, to encourage what is ultimately in the welfare of the individuals.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: That is why I had two recommendations in my speech yesterday: one is to introduce a base fee; two is to take cancellations and rejections of orders during bad weather out of the performance of the workers.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I understand what the Senior Minister of State said just now about not micromanaging the situation, but can I get a sense or a commitment whether the Government will encourage these two issues to be brought up in a negotiation at the platform work associations.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I think currently, the rule is rather onerous.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Once you opt in, you cannot opt out.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Is it possible for the Government to consider that maybe the platform worker, after they have opted in, whether they can reconsider the decision after a certain period, maybe on an annual basis?

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: But we have to take the approach of what is practical, how easy it is to implement and what cost it will be to the system overall.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: It may well be that some operators will have different models that they have agreed on with the operators and they can see that as a way of advantage to attract more workers who like that kind of arrangements to work for them as well.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This also maintains a competitive landscape among the different operators.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: But I would say also on the other aspect of opting in and out, whether it is time-dependent or a black-out period, whichever the construct may be, there will be quite a lot of challenges to implement because a particular platform worker could have been registered with several apps.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: If they are on several apps and they choose to opt in and out, each time they make a decision, it is not just one operator that has to make system changes and incur administrative costs, all the apps that this person has signed up with, even if it is an app that he uses very infrequently, would have to then also reflect that same CPF opt-in or opt-out status.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, as a system, it becomes very complicated and the cost is not borne by just one operator, it will be borne by quite a number of operators.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: I think the complex nature of this work is such that people can sign up for an app and not use it for a long time, but suddenly can use it again for a few months in a row.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, the very difficult nature of this sector is such that we try to keep things as simple as possible and reduce the overall cost burden.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: As I said in my speech, the solutions that we propose may not be 100% perfect, but the fact is that this legislation aims at providing the basic protections that will level up the protection for this group of workers, for it to be at least as close to being on par as possible with other employees working in a similar sector and also earning a similar income.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: In terms of achieving retirement adequacy and housing adequacy, we think this is a good base to start from.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: For any other operational benefits and challenges that may come along the way, we created the representation framework to allow negotiations and discussions to take place on a bilateral basis.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Senior Minister of State Koh, on the Bill proper, the first question pertains to the costs and how the costs will be distributed amongst platform operators, workers and we know the contribution of the Government.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: So, it is actually the flow-through, which is a bit more of a concern.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I think Member Mariam Jaafar today spoke about how different platform companies have their own models – some 0% and they will charge platform fees and so on, for example.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: So, there is a concern that for some platforms, there will be an incredible flow-through of these costs to the consumers; others, less so.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Does the Government have any expectation of how it is going to manage the situation such that platform operators do not willy-nilly just proceed and transfer all these costs accordingly to the consumer?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: My understanding is there is some concern about the cost of WICA for platform companies.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: As I iterated in my speech with three months to go before the introduction of WICA for platform workers, is there some landing insofar as how these premiums are priced, in view of the varied nature of the platform space?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Some clarity on that would be helpful because if WICA is very expensive, then one can imagine what the cost for the consumer would be.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So long as it is not monopolistic, there will be competition – competition for drivers, riders and competition also for customers.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: When that dynamic competition takes place, each platform will have to make sure that the cost that they are prepared to flow through, whether it is to the driver or to the customers, will have to be something that remains attractive to them both.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Otherwise, they will lose either the share of available labour or they will lose the share of the available market.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: But many of the things that we talked about – cost of CPF on operators and cost of WICA on operators – these are numbers that can be audited.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: For example, because now all platform workers will need to at least pay MediSave and those who opt-in or are mandated will have to pay CPF to their Ordinary and Special Accounts, which means that at the backend, we will know, by working backwards, what is the total wage cost that a particular operator with a particular load of workers will be paying for CPF or their wages.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: In that case, we can then determine the true wage costs for each operator and can audit and see if there is some evidence of profiteering.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: But I think, over time, with real world data, and now that we know who is a platform worker once the Bill comes to pass, the true incident rate of injuries and the severity of injuries being reported will allow more accurate actuarial data and claims history to be established over time.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, insurers then will have some real data to make some adjustments to the insurance premium that they charge.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: In a competitive market, if there are more than five, seven, maybe even more insurers who are prepared to come in – today, there are 26 operating in the employee WICA space – if a certain number of them also continue to participate in this for platform workers, we think the competitive premiums will continue to keep the market viable in terms of cost to operators.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Again, that part of the cost is also auditable, to determine how much it costs operators to put forth WICA compensations.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: A lot of people may think that WICA is charged on a per individual basis.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: But actually, the insurers look at this on a total wage cost basis.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, it is based on what the company is paying in terms of wages to their workers and the premium is calculated as such.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, it is irrelevant how many platform workers actually work for a particular platform company.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: What is more relevant is how much they are actually paying for the cost of wages to these workers that determines the WICA cost that they are paying in terms of premiums.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: My understanding is if the WP becomes the government of the day, then "we, the Workers' Party", according to Mr Gerald Giam, will partner unions.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Yet, Mr Giam says that you do not want NTUC to be tethered to the Government or PAP.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I do not think you can have your cake and eat it.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We use the words "partnership", "alliance", "solidarity" and "equal partnership".

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In the middle of COVID-19, we had multiple difficulties with the occupancy rates in hotels.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I had the privilege of being the advisor to the Food, Drinks and Allied Workers Union, or FDAWU.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: They were down one quarter occupancy rate, half occupancy rate.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Never in the meetings was there a subordinate-and-elder relationship.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It was about how we get our workers in their jobs through the pandemic, secure and get Singapore's economy afloat.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, on two points, I disagree with the hon Member Gerald Giam, from personal experience.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Number three, where was the partnership between PAP and NTUC formed?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Mr Lee Kuan Yew represented the Postal Workers' Union.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And why should we not rely on such trust, solidarity, mutual respect, equality, mutual relationship in advancing Singapore's cause?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It makes no sense, except if you dissect Mr Giam's position as being completely political.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, woe to those who disregard the past, especially if they seek to lead the future.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: Why are these council advisors appointed by the NTUC and why do they all happen to be PAP members or PAP MPs even?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: If I may, Sir, tripartism is a bedrock of Singapore's economy – the employers, the Government, the employees.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: I have been an MP for a number of years.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: When I go overseas, people ask: why are your unions not fighting against your government?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: The only conclusion I can draw, in my limited human mind, is that Mr Giam is a making a political point, whereas in my humble priority, it is Singapore that remains the priority.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I think it may be useful for a third party to come in and say a few words, and also to demonstrate that there are benefits of having a third party in this Parliament.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Leong, just confine it to this debate and not start a new one.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: First of all, I must speak out in support of the WP, what Members Gerald Giam and the Leader of the Opposition and the other Members have said.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I do not think the opposition is not in support of tripartism.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: In fact, no political party who aspires to run the country one day, would not want the support of the trade unions.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: All of us know history, that trade unions in other countries and by nature of their organisation, they must have the political power to institute change in a country.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, as a result, trade unions will want to be affiliated with political parties.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: And, of course, the opposition, whether it is the WP – of course, I cannot speak for the WP too much – but the PSP, for example, we would welcome, we want to cultivate the most harmonious and the best working relationship with trade unions.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, as a result, you cannot deny our impression.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: No opposition, few opposition politicians are being given appointments in NTUC and all that.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, we do not really understand the exact decision-making process there.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But from the structure that you can see from the outside, if the NTUC Secretary-General is a Minister or a former Minister and there are many leaders in the NTUC who come from the ruling party, I think we are entitled to think that the independence of NTUC ought to be better than this.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: I would appeal to Members on both sides of the House to again spare a thought about the unique position, the unique model that we have, the very special model that we have here in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We have been able to move, we have been able to progress so well.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This approach is fundamentally built on trust, on collaboration and a shared commitment to finding win-win solutions.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Through our decades of strong tripartite relationship between the unions, SNEF and the Government, collectively, we do not just talk, we do not just debate.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Together, we have robust discussions, we push back, we have intense debate behind the scenes.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: When we formulate ideas, we turn them into actions and we overcome challenges as one united people.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This unique approach is one of our greatest strengths.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Take, for instance, it was just barely two plus years ago, when we went through the crisis of our generation, COVID-19.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: When the crisis hit, the partners acted swiftly to address tough issues like cost-cutting measures, retrenchments.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This is in stark contrast to many other countries where tensions flared.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: It protected not just our lives, but our livelihoods.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: That is what is unique about our tripartism – that it works and it is a very, very unique, yet a true partnership.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The Government plays a key moderating role, of course, balancing the interests of both workers and businesses to ensure that all decisions, when they are taken, are made for the long-term good of everyone.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: I know you keep talking about independence, independence, independence.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Behind closed doors, the tripartite partners do not always agree.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Heated discussions happen behind closed doors on many, many issues – the raising of retirement age, or even the upcoming workplace fairness legislation.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: I am sure we will have another very intense debate during that time.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The Leader of the Opposition is already smiling at me, probably thinking, "You better watch it."

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We all work hard to reach a consensus, knowing that collectively we are always working for Singapore's shared interests.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And as I have said yesterday, not just for you, but for your children, for your grandchildren and hopefully, for your great-grandchildren.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: To quote Dr Robert Yap, the former President of SNEF, he once shared an anecdote with me when I just joined the Government.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And I thought that resonated and illustrated very well.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: He said it at a meeting with a foreign counterpart.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The foreign counterpart commented to Dr Robert Yap, the then President of SNEF, saying that he was lucky because Singapore's unions were weak because they do not strike.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Our outcomes, our positive outcomes are achieved through negotiation – not confrontation, not open confrontation.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: To paraphrase the late US Supreme Court Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg: do you throw away your umbrella in a thunderstorm because you are not getting wet?

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Members of the House, the lack of open confrontation, your so-called being more independent, does not mean that our unions are weak.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: It shows the power of positive collaboration in delivering results without disruption.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I urge all Members of the House, we are here to help our platform workers.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We are here and we have just finished and heard the wrap-up speech of Senior Minister of State Koh on how we can help our platform workers better, taking into consideration all of the comments, the suggestions, the opinions of Members of the House.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Let us not detract ourselves from this Bill.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I hope that you do not judge NTUC or SNEF by what you think the relationship between unions, employers and the Government should be.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: But look at the record, look at the outcomes, the positive outcomes that tripartism has delivered for Singapore through the decades.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Together, we have protected jobs, we have created stability, we have ensured prosperity for our workers, our businesses.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I hope we can continue to use this platform to support sustained tripartism as our competitive advantage, because by working hand-in-hand, we are not just navigating today's challenges, we are also securing a better, a brighter, a more secure future for Singapore and Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I hope that is the legacy that we must preserve.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: We have had a long debate and I think all the clarifications have been asked and answered.      .

text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 4.40 pm.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: The platform economy has provided opportunities to earn a living for many platform workers who bring convenience to us through their services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: During the COVID-19 pandemic, while most of us were safely working from home and observing safe management measures safely in our homes, many platform workers braved the elements and health risks to deliver goods and services and food items to us.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Following the pandemic, there is broad social support that we need to do more for this group of workers who have been left behind.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: First, platform workers generally have modest incomes that can fluctuate from month to month.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Second, they are also exposed to risks, such as traffic accidents, due to the amount of time they spend on the roads.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Those without sufficient insurance coverage bear the financial risks of getting injured and being unable to work.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Many of us in our Meet-the-People Sessions would have come across our residents who work as platform workers who sustained injuries at work and ended up with financial hardships and inability to service their housing loans.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: In fact, a 2022 poll by the Institute of Policy Studies found that up to a third of food delivery workers have been in at least one accident that required medical care.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Third, platform workers also have less control over their work, compared to typical self-employed persons.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: For instance, they may not have a say over how much to charge for their services, what tasks to take on, whether they can grow their own base of clients and so on.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: This is because platform operators control these decisions as part of their business models.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: When we say, "Every Worker Matters", we are recognising the inherent value and dignity of these workers, regardless of the work that they do.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: We are saying as a society that we are taking a stand – that these platform workers also deserve our care, to ensure fairness and equity.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Why should a platform worker who takes the same risks on the road as any other employee working in the delivery or transport sector be denied a fair compensation when they are injured or, worse still, lose their lives at work?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Are their lives worth less than other workers in the same sector?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Their work generates revenues for the platform operators.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Just as the platform operators pay Central Provident Fund (CPF) and buy workplace insurance for their staff working in their office, should these workers who brave the elements to ensure the revenue stream for the platform operators not get the same level of support and protection?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: I am glad that platform operators, workers and the broader society agree that we ought to do more for these workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: This is how we strengthen our social compact and not leave these workers behind as the platform economy continues to evolve and grow.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Therefore, to strengthen protections for those involved in platform work, the Ministry of Manpower (MOM) set up the Advisory Committee on Platform Workers (PWAC) in 2021 to review how ride-hail and delivery workers can be better supported in the areas of (a) housing and retirement adequacy; (b) financial protection in the case of work injury; and (c) representation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: These are some of the employment rights that employees have today.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: The PWAC consulted extensively, including with platform workers, companies, trade associations and academics, and examined international practices.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: This is a good example of how tripartite partners in Singapore have worked closely together to enhance labour standards in a sustainable manner.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Through close collaboration and discussions in the PWAC, tripartite partners have extensively and actively engaged key stakeholders, such as platform operators and platform workers, and effectively represented their perspectives in ironing out the policy and implementation details.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: There are four key components to the Platform Workers Bill.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: First, the scope of entities, including companies and workers covered under the Bill.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Second, measures to support the housing and retirement adequacy of platform workers through the CPF system.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: These involve amendments to the Central Provident Fund Act, or CPF Act.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Third, measures to ensure financial protection of platform workers if they get injured at work and to strengthen stakeholders' responsibilities to prevent injuries.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: These involve amendments to the Work Injury Compensation Act (WICA) and the Workplace Safety and Health (WSH) Act.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Fourth, the legal framework for representation of platform workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: This involves amendments to the Industrial Relations Act.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: These matters also require consequential and related amendments to a wide range of other Acts as well as the Constitution through the Constitution (Amendment) Bill, which will be tabled at a later Sitting.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: On the scope of entities covered, in clause 4 of the Bill, a platform operator is defined as an entity that has an agreement with one or more service users to provide platform services and exercises management control over one or more platform workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: We are covering ride-hail and delivery platform services as around 93% of platform work is concentrated in these services today and because such work is precarious, as I explained earlier.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: These platform services are set out in the First Schedule of the Bill.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: We can consider the need to amend the Schedule to cover other platform services in future reviews.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: In clause 6 of the Bill, there are two prongs to management control.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: If both are satisfied, the entity will be deemed a platform operator.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: First, platform operators use data from service users, such as consumers, as well as their workers in a highly, if not fully, automated manner to make decisions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: For instance, this could be through the use of algorithms that determine the fee that ride-hail drivers will receive for a trip based on data on the demand for rides and supply of drivers at a given time.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: The use of data in an automated manner to make decisions is a critical point here as it enables a platform operator to scale its operations significantly and quickly as well as impose and rapidly change terms of work for platform workers, with little or no room for negotiation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: The European Union's (EU's) directive on improving working conditions in platform work uses the same concept to define a digital labour platform.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Second, platform operators impose requirements, prohibitions or restrictions on their workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: These include imposing rules on how a task should be performed or restricting workers' ability to negotiate their fees with clients for providing the service.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: The effect of all these is that platform workers cede some autonomy to platform operators in terms of how they provide services, which makes them resemble employees to an extent.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: However, unlike employees, platform workers are not given employment rights.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: This is why we are moving to legislate some rights for platform workers to better support them at work.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Looking internationally, countries have taken different approaches to determine the statutory rights of platform workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Countries like Spain, Belgium and Portugal have presumed certain groups of platform workers to be employees, entitling them to employment rights, including fixed hourly wage, sick pay and vacation leave.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: But this means that they also lose the flexibility they had, such as deciding when and how much to work.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Some countries like Greece have presumed that platform workers are not in an employment relationship, but have given them some rights pertaining to welfare, health and safety, similar to employees.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Others such as the United Kingdom (UK) have left it to the courts to determine whether platform workers are "employees" or "workers" on a case-by-case basis.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: This led to different classifications for the same worker who may use different platforms to work.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: We want to better support platform workers by providing them with workplace safety and retirement adequacy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: But if platform workers are given the full suite of employment rights, such as sick pay and vacation leave, the nature of the relationship between the platform operators and platform workers will likely change to resemble an employment relationship, with much less flexibility, which neither party wants.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: We have thus struck a finely balanced middle ground.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: This approach preserves the flexibility of platform work that both sides want and achieves our aim of better protecting platform workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: The same applies to: (a) new companies; (b) existing companies that change their business models later on; and (c) companies in subcontracting arrangements if the company satisfies the definition of a platform operator vis-à-vis a worker.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Just like how companies today are responsible for assessing whether they are an employer and need to comply with employment laws, companies are also responsible for assessing whether they are a platform operator as they would be the most familiar with their own business models and their relationship with their workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: That said, to support companies, MOM will provide resources such as a checklist for companies to self-assess if they are platform operators.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Tripartite partners will also engage the ground to educate companies and relevant workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: If there is feedback that a platform operator has self-assessed wrongly and did not provide work injury compensation or make CPF contributions to a platform worker, MOM will investigate.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: If we find out that the company is a platform operator, we will require the platform operator to pay any outstanding CPF contributions or work injury compensation owed to the worker, as we currently do with employers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Additionally, the platform operator may face penalties for not making CPF contributions or not providing work injury compensation in a timely manner for platform workers and for failing to notify MOM that they are a platform operator.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Next, let me talk about supporting housing and retirement adequacy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: The Fourth Schedule of the Bill makes amendments to the CPF Act to support the housing and retirement adequacy of platform workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Today, platform workers are treated as self-employed persons and are only required to make MediSave contributions of up to 10.5% of their net earnings.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: To meet their housing and retirement needs, platform workers should also contribute to their CPF Ordinary and Special Accounts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: The proposed amendments enable platform workers to achieve the same level of housing and retirement adequacy as employees who earn the same amount.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: This will increase by the respective percentage quantum yearly until 2029.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: By then, it will bring platform operators' and workers' CPF contribution rates to the same level as employees and employers' contribution rates – by 2029.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: For platform workers in the ages of 55 to 65, the timing of the increase will be synchronised to the senior worker CPF contribution rate increases for employees in the same age group.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: The increased CPF contributions will be mandatory for the cohort of platform workers born from 1995 onwards.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: In all our engagements, younger cohorts have indicated the greatest need and desire for CPF contributions as it can help with their housing needs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Many are starting their families and getting their first Build-To-Order (BTO) flats.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Older cohorts can choose to opt in anytime from November onwards, with no deadline.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: I encourage older platform workers to consider opting in to boost their housing and retirement savings and to benefit from our CPF system.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Overall, platform workers will experience an increase in their total earnings after factoring in CPF contributions from platform operators.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Nonetheless, I appreciate that some platform workers will be concerned about reduced take-home pay.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: First, we will enhance the Platform Workers CPF Transition Support (PCTS) to provide greater support to lower-income platform workers who see an increase in their CPF contributions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: This means that the Government will pay fully for these platform workers' increased CPF contributions and they will have no decrease in their take-home pay in 2025.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: We will also enhance the offset in 2026 from 50% to 75%.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: The offset will taper down gradually thereafter and cease in 2029.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: We will also increase the PCTS qualifying income cap from $2,500 to $3,000, in line with the increase in the Workfare Income Supplement qualifying income cap from January 2025.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: This will allow more platform workers to benefit from PCTS.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Second, we will enhance Workfare for lower-income platform workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Today, platform workers are treated as self-employed persons for Workfare payments.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: This means that those who are eligible for Workfare receive Workfare payments annually, at the end of the year, after making their annual CPF contributions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: As self-employed persons today, they receive two-thirds of the Workfare payments that employees receive, as they make lower CPF contributions than employees, and 10% of Workfare is paid in cash and 90% goes to their CPF account.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: But from 2025 onwards, after this Bill is passed, platform workers will receive Workfare payments monthly, instead of annually, because they will now make CPF contributions on a monthly basis.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: As an illustration, for example, a 35-year-old platform worker earning $3,000 in net monthly income after deduction of allowable expenses, who opts in to increase CPF contributions from 2025, will receive around $2,250 of PCTS over the four-year period between 2025 and 2028, which will offset part of his increase in CPF contributions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: He will also receive $18,720 in CPF contributions from the platform operator over a five-year period from 2025 to 2029.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Including Workfare payments, the platform worker will receive a total of $23,830 in additional cash and CPF savings for his work from 2025 to 2029.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: So, this will be a substantial boost to the retirement adequacy and the ability to afford housing for these workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: All this will be helpful towards their housing mortgage payments and retirement savings.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: We have consulted platform operators and platform workers extensively in the design of the computation and collection of CPF contributions from them.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: We want to ensure that the CPF contribution process is seamless, cost-effective and protects the interest of platform workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: We have aligned generally with the employer-employee model while catering for flexibilities to account for the unique circumstances of platform work.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: These implementation parameters will apply to all platform workers, including those who have not opted in and only make MediSave contributions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Amendments to the CPF Act will specify how the computation of CPF contributions for platform operators and workers will be aligned to the employer-employee model in terms of how it is tiered based on age and income, and applied to monthly earnings from each platform.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Both platform workers and platform operators have provided feedback that they want a simpler and seamless way to compute CPF contribution.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: To this end, we will use a prescribed FEDA that reflects expenses for the majority of platform workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: The use of FEDA provides significant convenience for both platform workers and the operators, because the platform workers will not have to keep receipts to track and compute actual expenses for their platform work.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: The platform operators will not have to incur additional operating costs to re-compute the CPF contribution based on actual expenses.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: The prescribed FEDA also takes reference from the Fixed Expense Deduction Ratio developed by the Inland Revenue Authority of Singapore for the computation of net earnings for tax purposes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: This is based on actual expense ratios, including industry feedback and surveys on workers' expenses, and reflects expenses for the vast majority of platform workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: The use of FEDA will apply for the computation of work injury compensation as well.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Next, let me talk about the collection of CPF.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: During the month, the platform operator may make deductions and refunds to the platform worker based on the applicable CPF contribution rate.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: It is an offence for platform operators to make a deduction from a platform worker's earnings and not pay it to the CPF Board.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Platform operators will be required to reflect the deduction of the platform workers' share of CPF contribution clearly within their earnings slip for transparency and accountability and platform workers can check these contributions in their CPF account.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: The Fifth Schedule of the Bill carries amendments to the Income Tax Act to align the tax reliefs and deductions for CPF contributions to the employer-employee model.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: This is at clause 105 of the Bill, which amends the Child Development Co-Savings Act.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Today, before the Bill is passed, eligible platform workers get reimbursement from the Government for their lost income when they take parental leave.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: The Government does not reimburse them for any platform operator share of CPF contribution because this is not applicable to them today.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: This is part of Government's strong commitment to support parenthood.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Platform workers' financial protection for work injury is currently inadequate compared to employees in similar sectors, such as logistics.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Delivery employees and goods delivery partners both ply the roads to get deliveries to us and are exposed to the same risks.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Some platform operators voluntarily compensate platform workers for work injuries, such as through personal accident insurance.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: But the coverage is uneven and at lower levels than what employees are entitled to under WICA.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: It is important that platform workers, like employees, can recuperate and recover from their injuries without worrying about putting food on the table and get back to work in good health.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: The Ninth Schedule of the Bill will amend WICA in relation to platform workers and platform operators.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: The same compensation caps and minimum sums for compensation for permanent incapacity or death for employees will now apply to platform workers after the Bill is passed.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: To assure platform workers of work injury compensation payouts and to ensure platform operators can discharge their liabilities, platform operators will be required to purchase work injury compensation insurance for their platform workers from MOM-designated insurers.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Members may also access these materials through the MP@SGPARL app.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: I will focus on three areas: exclusions, what stage of the work is covered under the WICA and which platform is liable in the case of injuries.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Given the flexibility of platform work, liability for work injury compensation should be scoped to risks that stakeholders can practically address.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Some platform workers take platform work as their main job and do this throughout the day, while others do so on a part-time or ad hoc basis.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: As platform workers do not have fixed working hours or conventional workplaces, the circumstances under which platform workers will be eligible for work injury compensation will be more scoped, compared to employees.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The work injury compensation regime needs to account for the unique features of platform work.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: In a typical day, a platform worker would log onto the platform app to wait for jobs, before accepting a suitable job.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Then, the platform worker would set off to pick up the ride-hail passenger or the item to be delivered and complete the ride or delivery.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Hence, we can divide platform services broadly into three stages: waiting for jobs, picking up goods or passengers, delivering and completion of tasks – three stages.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: With reference to paragraph 31 of the Ninth Schedule of the Bill, amendments to the WICA specify the work stages of platform services.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: These are the key activities that take place after a platform job has been accepted.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Outside pick-up and delivery, platform workers can wait for jobs or pursue their own activities.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: It would not be fair to extend platform operators' liability to activities which are not work-related.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Which platform is liable in case of injury?

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: For platform workers injured while performing tasks for different platform operators at the same time, liability will be confined to one platform operator where possible to simplify claims processing.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This will be determined by a prioritisation of the work stages.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: First, if the platform worker was performing "pick-up" and "delivery” tasks for different platform operators at the same time, only the platform operator behind the "delivery" task will be liable.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This is because the platform worker can still choose to reject jobs during the "pick-up" stage but he or she is committed to fulfilling the job at the "delivery" work stage when the passenger or goods are already with them.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: If multiple platform operators are liable, liability will be apportioned based on the platform worker's earnings from each liable platform operator.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: For example, if the platform worker earned $1,000 from platform operator A and $2,000 from platform operator B, A will bear one-third of the compensation liability and B will bear two-thirds of the compensation liability.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: A platform worker could be performing work in two different platform sectors, meaning, both ride-hail and delivery.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Two different sectors: one is fetching passengers, the other one is delivering goods.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: If a platform worker gets injured while performing a task in a particular platform service, compensation will be based on the platform worker's past earnings from all platform operators that they had worked for in that platform service.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The platform worker's compensation will reference his earnings over a lookback period of 90 days before the date of the accident.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Platform workers injured while completing ride-hail and delivery jobs at the same time, that means, both platform services simultaneously, will be compensated based on the earnings from their higher-earning service sector.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Scoping platform operators' compensation liability to one platform service facilitates sustainable insurance premiums.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: While platform workers will be protected in case of work injuries, platform operators and workers should work together to reduce the possibility of work injuries in the first place and take remedial actions where necessary.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Today, all companies and workers are responsible for safety and health outcomes under the WSH Act.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Recognising the unique features of platform work, such as the use of different modes of transport for platform workers, we will introduce separate duties for platform operators and for platform workers through amendments to the WSH Act under the 10th Schedule.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This will clarify platform operators' responsibility for the safety and health of platform workers when at work and platform workers' responsibility to cooperate with platform operators on safety measures.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Today, a group of employees who want to represent their fellow employees must register themselves as a trade union and seek mandate to represent their members in negotiations with the employer and to resolve disputes.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Many of the challenges encountered by the platform workers are actually operational in nature and would be better resolved collectively through representative bodies that could work with various stakeholders including mall operators, food and beverage (F&B) chains and so on to find a good solution.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: As the framework for employers and employees has worked well in preserving industrial harmony, the Bill largely adopts this framework for platform operators and platform workers.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: In other words, platform work associations will be analogous to trade unions.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: First, we will appoint a Registrar and Assistant Registrars of platform work associations under clause 20 to assess the applications of platform work associations for registration and ensure the responsible administration of platform work associations.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Similar to how trade unions may represent employees or employers, platform work associations can represent platform workers or platform operators.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Once registered, the platform work associations of platform workers must obtain mandate from their members working with a platform operator to represent them in negotiations with that platform operator.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Second, once a mandate is obtained, a platform work association can work with platform operators to discuss and agree on areas for negotiation.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Thus far, companies and associations have raised various areas that they may be interested in negotiating, such as safeguarding the health and safety of workers, how earnings are computed and more.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Given that platform work is quite diverse and dynamic, tripartite partners agreed to leave it to each platform work association and platform operator to decide on what to negotiate on, rather than to pre-determine a list of issues that they can or cannot negotiate.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Third, it is important to preserve industrial harmony in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Therefore, amendments to the Industrial Relations Act under the Sixth Schedule of the Bill will extend existing channels for dispute resolution to platform work associations and platform operators.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: For instance, disputes can be brought to MOM for conciliation, and if that fails, the dispute can be heard by the Industrial Arbitration Courts.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: While platform work associations can organise industrial action just like trade unions, any decision to organise industrial action must be a considered and justified decision.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This is similar to the framework which governs trade unions today.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: We recognise that there may be concerns around costs arising from these measures.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The Government will put in place measures to manage the impact on stakeholders.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: For work injury compensation, the existing open and competitive insurance market for work injury compensation insurance will facilitate sustainable insurance premiums for platform operators based on the claims history and safety records.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Today, there are 26 insurers offering competitive insurance products for the employee regime.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: We have worked with seven of them to develop operational policies as part of the Platform Workers Work Injury Compensation Implementation Network including providing data for more accurate risk assessment, reducing uncertainty for insurers and platform operators.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: We will also introduce the enhanced PCTS for lower-income platform workers.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: To mitigate concerns around costs being passed down to platform workers, there will be provisions under the amended CPF Act and WICA that prohibit platform operators from recovering the cost of the platform operators’ share of CPF contributions and work injury compensation from platform workers, similar to existing provisions that apply to employers.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Consumers also have a critical role to play.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The introduction of CPF and workplace injury compensation protections will unavoidably lead to some increase in business costs, but I think as a society, if we all believe that we should provide some core protections for our platform workers, we should be prepared to pay just a little bit more to help platform workers secure their future.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: In fact, our surveys show that many consumers are indeed prepared to do so and I am heartened by this reflection of our strong social compact.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: (In Mandarin):   The platform economy has created opportunities for platform workers to earn a living and made life more convenient for many Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Platform workers born in 1995 and later will be required to contribute to their CPF Ordinary and Special Accounts.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Younger platform workers have expressed interest in making additional CPF contributions to meet their housing needs.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Older platform workers may already have their own housing and retirement plans, so they can choose to opt-in.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Platform workers' total income, including CPF, will increase.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: I understand that some platform workers may still be concerned that their take-home pay will be reduced.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: To address this, we will provide support to help low-income platform workers.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This means that the platform workers' take-home pay will not be affected next year.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The subsidy in 2026 will also be increased from 50% to 75% and will be gradually reduced in subsequent years.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Compensation includes medical expenses, income loss compensation for sick leave and hospitalisation and a one-time compensation for permanent incapacity or death.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Lastly, we will also establish a legal framework to allow platform work associations to represent platform workers, similar to how unions represent employees.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Singapore is one of the first countries to provide statutory protections for platform workers as a distinct group from employees.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Many other jurisdictions are similarly grappling with the challenge of how to better protect their platform workers.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: In this regard, the International Labour Organization (ILO) has reached out to Singapore to better understand our considerations and experiences in making these policy changes.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This signals how important this issue is and shows that we are at the vanguard of developing innovative and sustainable ways to better protect these workers.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: As Singaporeans, we can all be proud that we are doing this to uplift the social security protections for our platform workers who face precarity due to the nature of platform work.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The measures in the Bill will improve their housing and retirement adequacy, provide them with financial protection for work injuries, and enable platform work associations to act as a bridge between platform operators and platform workers so that industrial relations remain stable and conducive to the platform economy.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This would not have been possible without our tripartite partners and the close tripartite collaboration we have in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Everyone must play their part, including platform operators, platform workers and consumers at large.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The Government will also put in place transition measures to support stakeholders in implementing these changes.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Committee's recommendations sought to strengthen protections for platform workers in three areas: adequate financial protection in case of work injury through the Work Injury Compensation Framework provided by WICA, improved housing and retirement adequacy through CPF contributions, and finally, enhanced representation for platform workers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I will first speak on the platform workers space in general, and then on the higher prices for consumers that will most inevitably arise from the legislative changes effected by this Bill.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
