text: The second part of my speech will focus on specific queries on the introduction of CPF.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Before I speak on the substantive Bill, it is important to give an overview of the platform workers space and the incomes of our platform workers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The platform industry and how it is regulated, is also diverse.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For example, ride-hailing is far more regulated than food delivery, which is comparatively unregulated.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Another significant question concerning platform workers is whether they earn most of their income from platform work, or if such work merely supplements what they earn from their full-time jobs.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In a survey done as part of a 2022 Institute of Policy Studies inquiry on platform workers, 46% of respondents earned their income solely from food delivery, while another 27% earned income solely from platform work, including food delivery.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For a better understanding of each sub-category of platform workers, this figure needs to be parsed further so we can understand the median gross monthly income of each category of platform worker as listed by MOM, namely delivery workers, taxi drivers and private hire drivers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I hope the Ministry can provide this information so we can have an acute understanding of the income situation affecting specific type of platform work.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: With the cost of living biting Singaporeans at all levels, especially those of lower income, the earnings of most platform workers are precarious.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This view is reinforced by a 2023 DBS study, which showed that platform workers are spending more than they earn and have to tap into their savings as they try to cope with the cost of living.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This figure of 1.7 months is well below that of DBS Bank's median retail customer, who has savings of 3.5 months' worth of expenses.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It is also well below the 12 months' of savings recommended by DBS Bank's Head of Financial Planning Literacy for those with an unstable income stream.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Quite simply, many of our platform workers are potentially one major unexpected medical bill or even car repair away from exhausting their savings and sinking into real financial hardship.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The changes proposed by this Bill are aimed at helping platform workers by addressing their income and health-related insecurities.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This House understands, of course, that the changes provided by this Bill must be paid for by someone.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For now, there is little clarity on how much of the higher costs will be absorbed by the platform companies.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But the Bill will doubtless usher in a period of overall higher prices for customers of platform services.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: At a platform workers' dialogue session in 2023, Senior Minister of State Koh Poh Koon remarked, "All the surveys we have done, showed that Singaporeans are prepared to pay up to 10% more to support platform workers." However, a survey conducted in the first half of 2022, with a sample size of 2,000 respondents by the then-Ministry of Communications and Information (MCI) on how much consumers were willing to pay to facilitate better protections for platform workers, revealed more nuanced findings.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The MCI survey noted that four in five consumers were prepared to pay more for food delivery or ride-hailing services if the monies went to better support platform workers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Four in 10 respondents said that they were willing to pay up to 3% more, while three in 10 said that they were willing to pay 4% to 5% more.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: One consumer said that she was willing to pay a little extra, provided that the increase in costs were transparent and clearly went towards worker protection.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: A different survey in September 2022 of 570 respondents found that nine in 10 were prepared to pay more if the monies went towards initiatives to better support platform workers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Minister – through you, Mr Deputy Speaker – in view of the survey threshold and tolerance of Singaporeans for price rises for platform services arising from this Bill, how much does the Ministry anticipate prices to increase by and how will this be equitably spread between consumers, platforms and platform workers?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Specifically, after the implementation of the full CPF amount and WICA, are prices for users of platform services expected to rise by 5% or more, or will it breach the 10% mentioned by the Senior Minister of State?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Should the price increase be too high for consumers, one cannot rule out the prospect of a demand shock that causes consumers to recoil and reduce overall demand for platform services.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: If that were to happen, platform workers could find themselves with less work and even lower incomes.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In addition, does the Senior Minister of State expect platform companies to reveal how much of their anticipated price increases are accrued to the CPF and WICA amendments envisaged by this Bill?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Or are the algorithms of the platform companies expected to accommodate the increase in prices, with the public unclear about the extent of the price rise that is devoted towards better security for our platform workers?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The latter scenario may of course incentivise the prospect of profiteering in the name of regulatory compliance.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The next part of my speech covers questions on the preparations, assumptions and scenarios related to these new protections for workers, which are being brought to this House almost two years after the original recommendations of the Advisory Committee on Platform Workers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I will first speak on the compulsory CPF contributions for platform workers aged below 30, with an opt-in regime for platform workers above the age of 30.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In April 2022, I asked the Senior Minister of State Koh Poh Koon about the number of platform workers who contribute to their CPF accounts on their own accord.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It is not surprising that most platform workers do not contribute to their CPF accounts.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Anything that could reduce that amount is viewed with apprehension as it affects daily life.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: At a platform workers' dialogue session on 3 February 2023 involving about 120 workers, several workers raised their fears on whether the recommendations suggested by the Advisory Committee on Platform Workers would result in higher costs for platforms, which would then be passed on to workers, to the detriment of their take-home pay.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: One worker said, "I hope that it will not be the cost all (passed) over to us, (but) it will be spread across consumers, platforms and ourselves.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: At the end of the day, if you just say only and, when you implement, the cost come back to us, we are the ones paying the 17%." He was referring to the 17% rate for employers' CPF contributions.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Another worker alleged that the payment rate of the platforms had been decreasing since the announcement of the measures of the Advisory Committee on Platform Workers were made and asked, "How can the Government ensure that the platforms eventually don't give us the burden?" What is clear is that, platform workers are concerned about lower take-home income should platform companies extract the employers' contribution of CPF by adjusting the algorithm, thereby forcing take-home wages downwards.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The workers' concerns are in line with the public demand that the anticipated increase in the cost of platform services goes towards helping platform workers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I have a few queries for the Senior Minister of State on the CPF-related portion of this Bill.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: First, with an opt-in age of 30, most platform workers could choose not to participate.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Could the Senior Minister of State share the rationale and thinking of why it agreed to the opt-in age of 30, in view of the larger policy objective of addressing housing needs and retirement adequacy of platform workers?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Could the Senior Minister of State please tell us why the Ministry did not pursue an opt-out system, instead of an opt-in regime for those above 30 in age?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Opt-out systems, from a behavioural perspective, are far more effective in securing participation to address housing and retirement needs while yet giving choice to platform workers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In view of the life cycle of the CPF system and lower contributions received in one's later years, the early working years are important age brackets, during which, our platform workers can grow their CPF accounts to reap the benefits of compound interest in good time.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Considering that full-time employees are not even given the choice of either opting in or opting out, an opt-out system for platform workers does not seem inappropriate or unfair and would be far more effective in getting platform workers to seriously consider taking up CPF.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Fourthly, some platform workers are worried about whether they would be worse off if they opt into CPF as provided by this Bill.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: They are concerned that it would create a perverse incentive on the part of platform companies to assign more jobs to workers who are not making CPF contributions so as to lower the companies' wage expenditure.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Government needs to address this very real fear of our platform workers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Senior Minister of State Koh Poh Koon has previously stated that platform companies must not discriminate when assigning work and MOM would investigate any unfair practices.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Without more, my view is that this would be difficult, if not impossible, to prove discrimination as the evidence would lie in the word or, precisely, the algorithms of the platform companies.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It was reported that the Tripartite Workgroup on Representation for Platform Workers (TWG) had drawn up some negotiating principles with the platform companies, for example, (a) that parties would be mutually committed to the operators' business success and workers' welfare; and (b) platform operators need not divulge their proprietary information or negotiate on commercially-sensitive matters.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Can the Senior Minister of State tell us how the Ministry will investigate platform companies?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: How would the Ministry undertake investigations without access to the platform companies' top-secret algorithms, or does the Bill open the algorithms to scrutiny if discriminatory practices are alleged?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To address the fears of workers about falling incomes arising from the imposition of CPF, the Government announced the PCTS at the Committee of Supply debate in March last year.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Although, it must be noted that this would be the kick-off year where the workers' contribution is the lowest, at 2.5%.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Can I ask the Senior Minister of State, in the interest of fiscal transparency, what is the difference between the new fiscal allocation for the PCTS compared to the original PCTS announcement?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I move on to my queries on work injury compensation.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I have two broad queries in this regard.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: First, it would be important for this House to understand the deliberations of the work injury compensation implementation network for platform companies and workers, on the number of insurers, which I believe was briefly mentioned by the Senior Minister of State in his opening speech, and the cost of premiums to platform companies since there is a legitimate concern that added cost for platform companies with regard to WICA, are likely to be passed on to the consumer.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Have there been difficulties in pricing WICA for platform workers to date and do platform companies have a competitive range of quotes to consider?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: How many insurers are prepared to offer WICA, particularly since the product is new and the class of platform workers to be covered is far smaller than WICA for employees?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Separately, Mr Speaker, from the platform workers' perspective, for better work injury compensation, there must be a clear claims and compensation process for platform workers which is also easily understood.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It was made known in July 2023 that the compensation from income lost due to work injuries would be based on the worker's average actual earnings in the 90 days before the injury.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We see this all the time with platform workers toggling between several devices hosting different platform apps.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Could the Senior Minister of State please tell us whether a WICA claim would cover the 90-day average across all the platform companies a platform worker is registered with and works for no matter the number of jobs accepted over this period?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This is important because should a claim only be tied to the platform company, through which a platform worker accepted an assignment when injured, the WICA coverage for the worker may turn out to be very low.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Another point where clarification is needed, is the time frame during which a platform worker is considered at work.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For work injury compensation purposes, a platform worker is considered at-work during the pick-up and drop-off of passengers or items, including when they are headed to their vehicles or bikes.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: At least this is what I understood from the brochure that was circulated by the Senior Minister of State just now.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This means that the eligibility window for work injury claims opens when the platform worker accepts a job through their app and ends when they head to their vehicles or bicycles after finishing delivery.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Would there be scope to look at how WICA would apply to the completion of a food delivery job?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Usually undertaken by platform workers on motorcycles or bicycles, the risk profile of such platform workers differs considerably from platform workers who provide ride-hailing services.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Intuitively, the injuries sustained from even apparently minor accidents like brushes or side swipes involving two-wheelers can be severe, debilitating and, every so often, fatal.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Can WICA for platform workers accommodate and extend greater protection for our most vulnerable workers?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For example, can there be coverage if a food delivery rider completes a job, is in transit on the way home after a food delivery and, God forbids, gets involved in some serious accident?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I believe there is some scope for reviewing the applicability of WICA for food delivery riders and ride-hail platform workers differently, to better protect more vulnerable workers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This is worth consideration precisely because of the unconventional deployment of WICA in the ordinary sense, which is commonly extended to those traditionally classified as employees only.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I hope the Ministry can look into this.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Separately, in a Business Times article dated 13 July 2023, it was reported that a ride-hailing driver had a specific query on whether the WICA coverage would extend to platform workers who get into an accident while waiting for the app to assign new jobs.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: There was no clarity on this point in the article, so it would be helpful if the Senior Minister of State can address this point in the House, too.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Before moving on from this section, the incorporation of WICA for platform workers by way of this Bill does not mean that platform companies have been leaving workers in the lurch.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Foodpanda has extended skills upgrading schemes for its workers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: A few companies, such as Gojek, offer subsidised premiums if workers take up private insurance.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To that extent, I agree completely with the Senior Minister of State's explanation on WICA for platform workers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As iterated earlier, the tripartite discussions that preceded the Bill acknowledged that the business secrets of platform companies, such as the operational details of their matching algorithms, would be respected.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I believe many people in and out of this House would have heard platform workers speak of riders or drivers allegedly receiving notice of a job in the vicinity, while another driver or rider may not receive the same notice.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Unfortunately, these very algorithms that determine allocation are driven by the business strategies of the platform companies and one can understand that they may be trade secrets.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: While the House must respect the liberty of private enterprise to the extent possible, equally, it is important for platform companies to both proactively explain as well as publicise to their workers how important decisions, such as job allocation, performance assessment of workers and rates, are decided.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: A balance has to be struck between respecting business secrecy on one hand and the legitimate concerns of workers on the other.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Ultimately, any new status quo must better level the playing field between platform workers and platform companies to ensure that workers' rights are protected.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I would also like to ask the Senior Minister of State, if representation as effected by the Bill could co-exist with the prospect of platform workers sharing their data with an association.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In the UK, a non-profit entity called WorkerInfoExchange helps platform workers access and gain insight from data collected from them at work, with a view to tilting the balance away from big platforms by collecting and pooling the data of platform workers to help them demand fairer conditions.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Can the Senior Minister of State confirm if this Bill envisages a platform work association representing platform workers operating in a similar way, given there is an understanding that platform companies will not be expected to reveal the inner workings of their algorithms?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: If representation delivers a more level playing field for workers and information, asymmetries between workers and companies are reduced in a real way, more platform workers are likely to be assisted directly, where representation carries weight and bargaining power.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Protecting our platform workers is a cause the Labour Movement has championed for many years.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This Bill addresses the unique challenges faced by workers in Singapore's growing gig economy, now widely known as platform workers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: These workers have quietly become indispensable to our daily lives – delivering our food, driving us to our destinations and bringing parcels to our doorsteps.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: At its core, this Bill seeks to strike a delicate balance.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: On the other hand, this Bill is sensitive to the flexibility that characterises platform work.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The objective is not just to protect current workers but to ensure that the gig economy remains a sustainable part of our economy in the long term.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The cornerstone of this legislative change is Singapore's tripartism.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Tripartism is our unique collaboration among the Government, employers and unions.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It has long been the bedrock of Singapore's labour relations.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It is this spirit of cooperation and dialogue that has enabled us to achieve what many other countries have struggled with: a harmonious and effective approach to regulating and improving the gig economy.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In many countries, efforts to regulate the gig or platform economy have faced significant resistance.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In California, for example, platform companies have invested millions in legal battles to overturn legislation protecting platform workers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The situation has similarly been challenging in Europe, where attempts to classify gig workers as employees have been met with stiff opposition from platform companies.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: However, in Singapore, we have taken a different approach.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: By leveraging on our strong tradition of tripartism, we have brought together the Government, unions and platform companies to craft a framework that balances the needs of all parties.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This collaborative approach has allowed us to move forward with this bold legislative and policy change, ensuring we protect our workers while maintaining the flexibility and sustainability of the gig economy.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: A key feature of the Bill is ensuring that platform workers have access to CPF contributions.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This is crucial for helping them build a secure financial future, especially for younger workers who aspire to own their homes and save for retirement.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: By mandating CPF contributions from both platform companies and workers, we are not just protecting these individuals.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: While it may be challenging for workers to adapt to a lower take-home pay initially, the PCTS will help alleviate this burden.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This phased approach gives workers time to adjust to the new scheme.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Workers will also get employers' contributions to the CPF, lending further support for longer-term retirement and housing support.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: If we care for the workers, we must plan for the longer run.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Currently, mandatory work and injury compensation for platform workers is non-existent.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Some platform companies offer insurance but it is not mandated.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This leaves workers vulnerable when accidents occur, facing both medical bills and loss of income.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Cases of riders suffering injuries resulting in inability to work are not uncommon.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Without mandatory workplace injury coverage, they will have to rely on their savings or the goodwill of friends and family to cover their medical expenses and support their households.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Such is the precarious situation many delivery riders face.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The struggles underscore the urgent need for a standardised, mandated workplace injury compensation scheme that protects all platform workers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Whether it is a delivery rider injured at a job or a private hire driver involved in an accident, platform workers will now have the peace of mind that comes with knowing they are now covered.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The Bill also allows for platform workers to be formally represented by associations, giving these associations legal standing to advocate on behalf of workers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This is welcome news for the labour union-affiliated associations, like the National Private Hire Vehicles Association, the National Delivery Champions Association and the National Taxi Association.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: With the formal legal backing, these associations can now, more effectively, engage with platform companies to represent and protect their members, ensuring a more balanced playing field for platform workers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: And members will also be supported by NTUC's full ecosystem of support and privileges.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Without such representation, platform workers often find themselves voiceless and powerless.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In the UK, Uber drivers had to fight a lengthy legal battle to be recognised as workers, rather than independent contractors.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: These protections will likely come at a cost, at least in the short term.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Platform companies will need to adjust their business models to comply with these new obligations and some of these costs may, indeed, be passed on to consumers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The Government has come in via the PCTS to help with the transition.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This means that short-term price volatility is likely to be mitigated, giving time for the system to adjust.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: However, we must remember the broader social compact that we are trying to build in Singapore requires contributions from all parties.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: All of us, platform workers, companies and consumers, must share the responsibility of ensuring that the gig economy remains fair and sustainable for all stakeholders.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: By working together, we can ensure that these changes benefit not just platform workers, but all of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: There are a few points I would like to raise for the Ministry's considerations.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The gig economy often involves workers engaging with multiple platforms simultaneously.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For instance, a delivery rider might work for different food delivery platforms or even ride-hailing services, as discussed earlier.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This can create unique challenges when it comes to applying to WICA.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We have talked about having a look-back period, but invariably, this may lead to disputes among insurance or even companies delaying compensation for workers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The Bill primarily focuses on workers engaged in transportation and delivery services.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: But the gig economy clearly extends beyond these sectors.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Platforms offering cleaning services, digital work and nursing services are also significant parts of the gig economy.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Providing platform workers with the protection they deserve is essential as we build an inclusive society.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It also demonstrates that the People's Action Party (PAP) Government is prepared to make bold changes to its policies to improve the lives of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The gig economy offers workers a flexible way to achieve financial independence or sustenance, and we must ensure they are protected from the imbalances of power that exist in this sector.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We must continue to listen to the voices of our platform workers and make necessary adjustments to ensure that this Bill achieves its intended outcome.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Every worker matters and the Labour Movement stands ready to assist the Government in engaging our platform workers to ensure that this Bill achieves its intent.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I look forward to a stronger social compact, ensuring that our society works towards leaving no worker behind.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Many of our Sengkang residents work for these platforms in the gig economy, too, and I have spoken to quite a number of them during my Meet-the-People Sessions, house visits and our shopping malls where many of them are waiting for their next delivery pick-up.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The Labour Movement is no stranger to the ground concerns of our freelance workers and thanks to Singapore's unique style of tripartism, has been representing our workers' rights to the Government and platform taxi companies.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Successful negotiations through the tripartite partnership have helped our drivers and riders through challenging times and have created improved worker outcomes in terms of work prospects and working conditions.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We also innovated voluntary mediation for disputes with operators and we want to thank our progressive operators for their support.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Throughout COVID-19, we protected livelihoods by working with taxi companies to reduce rentals and hold taxi pump prices when fuel prices spiked.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Partnering closely with our food court operators, platform companies and the Government, NTUC negotiated on proper rest areas for drivers and riders providing essential services during the COVID-19 restrictions.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: These working models and Tripartite relationships have been carefully cultivated by our associations to improve the welfare of our workers in the absence of legislation.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: If Members need proof of this working model, it is visible here at the Gallery with our platform operators seated next to our platform workers.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, Mr Speaker, there are miles to go before we sleep, and as more Singaporeans choose to be part of the gig economy and as more global players enter this fast-evolving platform industry in Singapore, it is important that our workers' interests and livelihoods stay protected.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And we know that platform workers are stressed about the long-term sustainability of their livelihoods, especially with non-transparent incentives and order mechanisms, app glitches and fluctuating demand/supply.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: They are worried about unsafe working conditions and the financial burden placed on their families should accidents or even deaths occur.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: They are aggrieved over the lone voices they have when it comes to their challenges being heard by platform partners and other stakeholders in the course of their daily work.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Unlike the truly self-employed, today’s platform workers are in employee-like work arrangements as they are subjected to their platform operators' management controls and have to adhere to the platforms' rules of engagement.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Many a times, our platform workers are left in vulnerable situations especially when their platform partners change their incentive structures and order booking rhythms.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Brother Calvin, not his real name, was once a delivery rider using a power-assisted bicycle (PAB).

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Despite booking those same peak-hour shifts, fewer orders started coming in.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Once, he went for days without even being able to book for the same shifts he once used to be able to get.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Seeing that bicycle deliveries had shift slots opened when there are none opened for PABs for the same shifts, he resorted to changing his delivery method from PAB to bicycle.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The week-by-week change threw off his cadence in life, and I believe that livelihoods should not be as precarious and fleeting as an unconsulted, unconsented change in a partner platform’s priorities.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Calvin is fortunate that he was nimble enough to leave the industry, but there are scores of others in this industry, who have fully vested their livelihoods and trust in platform apps, finding themselves in a double bind.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: They are unclear why the rules of engagement on their partner platform have changed, while trying to make ends meet for their families in a job that had promised partnership and a viable means to a livelihood.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Indeed, representation also covers circumstances which may appear trivial to the rest of us, but bear great impact to our drivers and riders.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In my interactions with our delivery riders, many have brought up to me about the hump at most of our public carpark gantries.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While most of us cannot recall that hump, and I appreciate how the HDB has put these humps in to slow down cars before the gantry, the hump is a bane to many delivery riders as it causes the cream decoration on cupcakes to be overturned, and drinks to be spilled.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Our riders have told us that they often do not know where to bring these grievances to, hence tripartism and formal representation would be critical twin pillars in allowing our platform workers’ voices to be heard.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The fact of the matter is that workplace injuries are common in the delivery space and, more often than not, our platform workers leave behind grieving family members, finding themselves even in more precarious financial situations.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While we argue that many platform companies do provide basic insurance cover for their drivers and riders, as pointed out, these insurance are often inadequate and are uneven in coverage, many a times, tied towards performance metrics and tiered privilege systems.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I ask, should something as basic as insurance be gamified?

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Take the tragic example from June 2022, when a 54-year-old food delivery rider lost his life in an accident at the Punggol Waterway Point mall.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I attended his wake and what struck me most was the vulnerability of his family.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: He was the main breadwinner in the family, leaving behind an elderly mother.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The National Delivery Champions Association set up a counselling booth with the assistance of the mall to support the riders who witnessed the accident.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It was a reminder of how real the dangers is at work for our platform workers.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In the same vein, the same must be said of our platform workers’ CPF and housing adequacy.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Private hire vehicle brothers Joseph and Gabriel tell me that they find it difficult to maintain a steady stream of income due to the non-transparency of work order rhythms and the fluid nature of a platform's incentive system.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: They are both family men coping with the rise of business costs out of their control – rentals and petrol mainly – and the volatility of their platform earnings.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The pressures are compounded by the demands of their families and long-term commitments.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Our platform workers’ stresses are not unique and is commonly shared by all Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The difference is that for most working Singaporeans, they have the certainly in planning and growing a nest egg through CPF contributions.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Growing older means higher healthcare costs, growing a family means taking on housing loans.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Gabriel shares that the rental cost of a Toyota Noah that used to cost $80 a day pre-COVID-19 now costs $110.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This is a 37.5% increase, but definitely fares have not increased proportionately.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Today, he has to drive another one to three extra hours just to maintain his pre-COVID-19 income, but with a good sense of financial literacy and prudency, Gabriel is able to maintain his lifestyle to manage his family’s daily expenses.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, others might not be as savvy as Gabriel and some are now falling into arrears.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Indeed, anecdotally, just as I was receiving feedback from our member drivers on unsustainable low trip and order rates, I have also seen a corresponding higher number of platform workers in arrears for their HDB loans at my Meet-the-People Sessions in the past six months.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: These worries and aspirations are not only those belonging to our traditional breadwinners.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Our sisters have also often voiced out their needs for long-term financial adequacy for their families and themselves.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: These are not their real names – sister Farrah, a mum of six; sister Maria a single mum with an adult son; sister Courtney, a single mom with a child with disabilities, have all called for better housing and retirement adequacy.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Sister Farrah would like to purchase a flat of her own, sister Maria would like to contribute to her son’s future marital home and sister Courtney would like to provide better therapy services for her special needs child.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Our platform operators, as with all the rest of Singapore-based employers, will need to provide their share of CPF as part of their cost of business.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This will be critical in ensuring that our platform workers are paid fairly for a sustainable livelihood and be finally on par with the rest of the workforce for the work that they have done.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: My taxi and private hire vehicle association leaders have a wise saying: "羊毛出在羊身上".

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The sheep's wool must come from its body.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: (In Mandarin):   For over a decade, the Labour Movement has been listening to and representing the voices of freelancers and self-employed individuals in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: NTUC and its affiliated National Taxi Association, National Private Hire Vehicle Association and National Delivery Champions Association have been dedicated to promoting and planning this Bill for many years.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Through our Tripartite efforts, we are finally able to stand in Parliament today to debate this landmark Bill.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: If this Bill is passed, it will be a world first, formally recognising that platform workers can enjoy benefits similar to those of employees.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This way, platform workers can enjoy corresponding formal rights through platform associations.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: More importantly, it will ensure workers receive comprehensive work injury insurance and enhanced retirement and housing security.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Once platform workers can enjoy treatment similar to employees, they will be able to benefit from these basic benefits and rights.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We must take more measures to support this growing group in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: NTUC has deep concern for platform workers, and we will continue to safeguard their interests as we have always done, because we cherish every platform worker. : Mr Speaker, more must be done to support this growing group of Singaporean workers.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As I rise in support of the Bill, which the NTUC and the Labour Movement have worked hard to push, I reiterate, as I have on several occasions, the concerns I have with the roll-out.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Waiting in between bookings and jobs is a regular part of a platform worker’s daily job routine.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As long as a platform worker has his or her app on, and has exhibited that they are ready to take on a booking, arguably, this waiting time should also be covered under the work injury insurance.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The coverage can be capped up to $2,500 of their earnings.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As workers working in precarious work conditions, platform workers must be covered adequately by accident and loss of income insurance.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: NTUC cares deeply for our platform workers and we will continue, as we have done over the years, to champion their interests, because every platform worker matters.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: My clarifications not withstanding, I strongly support the Bill.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Speaker, the Platform Workers Bill is a comprehensive, even exhaustive, document, numbering some 234 pages, and addressing a wide range of legislative changes meant to enfold platform work better into the jobs landscape of our economy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It makes good-faith efforts to improve the rights and protections for gig workers, and for that reason, it has the support of the WP.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Others have already spoken about various other aspects of the Bill, including enabling such workers to secure representation via workers associations or union equivalents, along with accommodations for workplace health and safety.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I will, in my remarks, focus on how the Bill caters specifically to retirement adequacy of such platform workers, which is a principal concern of Part 8 of the Bill.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: For context, let me begin with a sketch of the economics of the platform economy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Digitally-oriented business models have been with us for a long time now, of course, having risen to prominence in the run-up to the dot-com boom of the late 1990s.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But it was only after the bursting of that bubble that we saw the subsequent emergence of both sharing economy firms such as Airbnb, Uber and WeWork, along with the penetration of incumbent technology giants like Amazon, Facebook and Google into such digital ecosystems and that has ushered in the current generation of platform economies.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The digital economy is now massive and will only continue to grow.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In Singapore, the Infocomm Media Development Authority expects a comparable share of the digital economy in our gross domestic product (GDP), with digital businesses outpacing the rate of growth of the overall economy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Yet the platform economy raises intimate issues of concern for workers in particular.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: What is worse, while some founders and employees at the top end – think of the thousands of well-remunerated tech professionals, not to mention tech billionaires like Jeff Bezos, Jack Ma and Mark Zuckerberg – have benefited enormously from the platform economy, tens of thousands of others are barely eking by, on precarious driving, delivery and paid-per-gig jobs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The present Bill limits itself to a class of workers providing on-demand delivery and ride-hailing services operating on digital platforms.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This, in my view, is an appropriate prioritisation, given their relative share of all platform workers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: After all, such workers reside in an awkward intersection of regular wage-earning employees, whose jobs afford sufficient structure for traditional labour protections and the fully self-employed who understand the risky trade-offs of running one's own shop but get to enjoy the potentially large returns from business success or the freedom of being one's own boss.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Unlike the self-employed, however, most platform workers cannot decide on how much they charge and many do not do gig work out of choice.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: They may be responding to, for instance, an unexpected job displacement or an inability to secure more traditional employment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This would include freelancers on Amazon Mechanical Turk or Fiverr, but also cleaners and handymen or performers that heavily rely on platforms to match themselves to work opportunities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Such individuals exhibit many of the same features of employment precarity that on-demand delivery and ride-hailing workers do.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Of course, the experiences of platform workers within this group may well differ, depending on their motivations for seeking work and even the specific platforms on which they operate.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While some are reasonably well-off and choose platform work as a helpful supplement to their primary income, most are on the lower end of the income scale and may suffer from significant income volatility, resulting in higher levels of job anxiety.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Many have to go into debt to even get started on gig work.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This has led some observers to criticise the claims that platform work fosters some special spirit of entrepreneurship as "utopian thinking".

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The reality, instead, is that many employees engaged in platform work full-time live very vulnerable economic lives.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The majority are bereft of health insurance or retirement plans or social protections, more generally.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The flexibility of gig work – often presented as a boon – is often a bane in reality as workers often cease work once they have reached a daily target, which in turn erodes their long-term earnings capability.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: A significant number are young – since the higher starting salaries may prove irresistibly attractive, relative to the alternative – but with limited career upside, lifetime incomes often end up lower than with conventional careers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Absent stronger incentives, a majority would either completely opt out of contributions towards CPF or make only minimal contributions to keep their take-home salaries high.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: As a result, many platform workers fail to squirrel away enough money to support themselves later in life.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Yet there is some evidence that platform workers may actually favour mechanisms that can help them commit, somehow, to increasing their savings, although this is of course tempered by a concern that the possibility of their take-home pay would decrease as a result.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is why it is vitally important to ensure that platform workers have access to a pension plan.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In Singapore, this typically means enrolling in the cornerstone of our system of retirement provision, the CPF.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: To be clear, the WP has in the past offered measured critiques of the system.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Notwithstanding these reservations, we believe that CPF goes some way towards providing for retirees during their sunset years and hence, has a role to play for platform workers as well.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Behavioural scientists have documented how a bias towards the status quo, coupled with inertia, tends to lead individuals to stay with pre-selected defaults.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This has also been demonstrated, specifically, when it comes to saving behaviour.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Hence, if we believe that it is truly beneficial to nudge our platform workers towards greater savings for retirement, applying an opt-out default would be no less constraining on their freedom of choice while encouraging welfare-enhancing behaviour.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: That said, as my hon friend Louis Chua has already and my friend Gerald Giam will, point out, the scheme could nevertheless give rise to unintended consequences as well.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Platform companies may tweak their algorithms to deprioritise job allocations for those who are contributing more to CPF or they may choose to blatantly reduce the salaries of those who sign onto the scheme.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Here, I raise the possibility of another possible unintended consequence, related to how those under 30 years of age are automatically enrolled in Group A.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While I can guess at the Government's motivation behind insisting that the young be automatically placed in Group A – it ensures that those who will benefit most by starting their retirement saving early do so and, as Senior Minister of State Koh earlier said, older workers may already have some savings plan in place – this may nevertheless inadvertently lead to discrimination against their hiring since they are now also more costly.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This may further exacerbate youth unemployment, which – like elsewhere in the world – is already more than twice as high as the adult unemployment rate.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This concern has already been flagged by some of our younger platform workers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The counter-argument that suggests that the number of workers not on the scheme is likely to be small – and hence, discrimination is not possible since most workers would be covered – does not hold up to the data.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And the belief that such a discriminatory strategy would not hold up in the longer run also does not address how a sizeable group of youths could nevertheless face discrimination in the meantime.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Nor should we be content with the claim that younger workers – being fitter, more resolute or more efficient – are naturally more attractive hires.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: After all, we are well aware of the weaker bargaining power of employees with less experience in the workplace, which may well predispose them to accepting otherwise lower wages than they deserve.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: One strategy to preclude this, without throwing the baby of retirement adequacy out with the bathwater of potential discrimination, is to ensure that the impending Anti-Discrimination Bill, which, last I heard, is due to be debated in Parliament this year, includes provisions that would make such unsavory practices illegal, notwithstanding the challenges of proving discrimination in practice that the Leader of the Opposition has pointed to.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Separately, one is left to wonder what the Government's Plan B is, should the enhanced PCTS fail to deliver the sort of sign-up rates that we all hope for.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: After all, while the lock-in into Group A for older workers who exercise the CPF scheme option is assured by clause 4(3) of the Fourth Schedule, such inevitability may well end up discouraging workers from signing up in the first place.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: These workers will nevertheless face retirement adequacy issues and hence, it strikes me as valuable to monitor the rate of sign-up as well as develop a strategy for encouraging participation in the event that the enhanced PCTS alone remains insufficient as an incentive.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: First, about the injuries incurred in the course of work.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I appeal to the Ministry to extend this protection beyond physical injuries.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Just like employees in the services industries, including the healthcare and security sectors, our platform workers require protection against verbal threats and psychological abuses.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This Bill does not address this prevalent issue but it is not uncommon to hear stories about platform workers being verbally abused for being delayed due to weather or traffic conditions.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Private hire vehicle drivers get berated for various reasons by passengers.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This can affect them emotionally or worse, financially, as they may be given bad reviews even though they are not at fault or for situations beyond their control.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, I am still very much concerned about their income progression and the stresses they face due to the volatility and unpredictable nature of their earnings, which are dependent on seasonal demand.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: There is a limit to how many orders or trips one can do a day, due to supply and demand factors, road conditions and physical human limits.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As these riders grow older or reach other milestones in life, how can we ensure their income goes up in tandem with inflation and/or be able to meet the expenditure needs for major life events?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: (In Mandarin):   There is a limit on how many orders or trips one can do a day.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This is due to supply and demand factors, road conditions and physical limits.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As these riders grow older or reach other milestones in their life, how can we ensure their income goes up in tandem with inflation and/or able to meet the expenditure needs for major life events? : Presently, food delivery and ride hailing companies have tiered systems for benefits.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Payment incentives are provided for a number of rides at each tier.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Those in the higher tier also have priority in booking shifts and getting orders.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: These incentives are not fixed and companies can always drop these incentives at their own discretion.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: There is no protection in terms of their stability of income.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: What more can we do to ensure that their incomes do not fall even if they are working just as hard?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: How do we ensure that their incomes rise over the years to keep up with inflation?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: At the same time, how can we balance this with keeping with the cost of such services affordable to the majority of our consumers?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is important that they can have career mobility and employability.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: How do we ensure the career mobility of our platform workers?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For platform workers who may at some point decide to move on from being a platform worker and find a more stable employment, the Government may wish to consider providing more support for platform workers to attend trainings, with some form of allowance or income support.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Such support should be a permanent feature and not ad hoc.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Today, platform workers provide much appreciated last-mile service, making a difference in terms conveniences in our daily lives; their services widen our dinning and consumption options, and they plug the service gap for those who are less mobile such as our seniors or those that are unwell.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Rain or shine, platform workers carry out their work; often under time pressure to fulfil their job orders.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: There is a lot of daily toil and hard work on their part.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: They, like the rest of us, also have their ups and downs in life, emotions, angst and anxieties.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Like us, they also have families and loved ones and they too want safety, security and better life for themselves and for their families.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: At Bukit Panjang where I served, we have a Delivery Riders Support group where we get together regularly such as during festivities, to catch up and to offer each other support and assistances.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In my frequent engagements with the platform riders, they will often share with me about what they are going through, the daily challenges that they face as well as their concern on the longer-term stability and security of their work as well as their longer-term livelihoods.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: So, in my view, the sector is still in search of the optimal financial equilibrium and yet to be on a more self-sustaining footing.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Do we expect the terms of trade between among the stakeholders which are the platform operators, platform workers, consumers and, in the case of food delivery, the F&B operators, do we expect any change in the terms of trade among the stakeholders as a result of this Bill?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is a significant portion of our workforce and many of them are lower income and have been displaced from the job market in recent years.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While platform workers generally enjoy more flexibility than employees, they are also subject to significant management control by platform companies when their supply of services are matched to demand by algorithms.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is timely that our legislation is now being updated to create a new class of workers distinct from employees and self-employed persons to protect the rights of platform workers.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is a step in the right direction which will ensure that younger platform workers have adequate protections for housing and retirement.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The opt-in regime for older platform workers also meets the desire of many older platform workers to opt out of CPF contributions on their earnings in order to maximise their take-home pay.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, in order to ascertain that this change will really benefit the platform workers, we would like to ask the Government if it has gotten commitments from the platform companies that they will not reduce incentives or earnings rates for platform workers to offset their increased cost from paying employer CPF contribution.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: During the Committee of Supply for MOM in 2023, my colleague Ms Hazel Poa had raised the issue of whether platform workers who opt in to CPF contributions will be discriminated against because they are more costly and asked whether measures were put in place to prevent discrimination against those who opt in.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: At the time, Senior Minister of State Koh Poh Koon clarified that platform workers would not be covered under the upcoming workplace fairness legislation and that it is not in the interest of the company to discriminate against workers who opt in for CPF because over time, the bulk of the workers available for platform work will need mandatory CPF.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, PSP is concerned that in the short term, there are insufficient protections to prevent Group A workers who opt in for CPF from being discriminated against.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We are disappointed that the Bill does not contain provisions to prevent platform companies from discriminating against Group A workers.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: PSP proposes that MOM should regularly receive reports from the platform companies on the percentage of jobs that are completed by Group A workers as well as the percentage of Group A workers on their platform.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: MOM should regularly monitor these data points to ensure that there is no evidence of platforms discriminating against platform workers who may be more costly because they opt in to CPF contributions.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We would like to go further to ask MOM to consider proposing the ultimate safeguard of a minimum base fare per delivery or right share.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We propose that platform workers can form platform work associations that functions similarly to trade unions.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A minimum base fare could be negotiated between the platform work associations and platform companies as part of the negotiations on the Collective Bargaining Agreement.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The PSP's view is that platform company and platform work associations should work towards an appropriate minimum base fare calculated with reference to our proposed living wage of $2,250 per month before CPF contributions for 44 hours of work per week.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While platform workers are viewed by some as independent contractors, the workers, overall compensation is to a large extent determine by the platform companies.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As a result, appropriate policy has to be set to ensure that platform workers are compensated fairly for their services.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The 2022 IPS survey Precarity in Platform Work, a study of private hire vehicle drivers and food delivery riders, found that more than 90% full-time private hire vehicle drivers across all age cohorts were worried that they will no longer able to earn enough money because the financial incentives given by platform companies are increasingly being cut or reduced.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: When deliberating this Bill after the First Reading, we were of the view that while equitable pay is important, it is also important to ensure the safety of our platform workers is not compromised by the pressure of work.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is a much better improvement over the voluntary work injury compensation coverage currently provided out of goodwill by platform companies.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We also note that the work safety of platform workers will be further strengthened by the draft code of practice for platform services, which the WSH Council has put up for public consultation last week.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Under part 4.5.1 of the code, platform companies should limit the load to be delivered to the capacity of the delivery bag and/or the maximum load weight of the vehicle or active mobility device.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The PSP supports this as it will better protect platform workers from being exposed to unsafe situations due to excessive loads.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, part 4.5.2 of the draft code of practice does not address the fact that platform workers may feel pressured into accepting jobs during unsafe weather conditions, because of the penalties imposed by platform companies on cancellations.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The PSP thus proposes that part 4.5.2 of the draft code of practice should be amended to include that platform companies should remove the penalties for workers who reject or cancel orders during bad weather conditions.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Such cancellations or rejection of orders should not be included when rating the platform workers' performance.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is not an extraordinary step because there is at least one major platform company, Deliveroo, that does not penalise riders in this way.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We hope that MOM will consider these suggested measures to ensure that this Bill and the code of practice will be more effective in ensuring a safer working environment for platform workers.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is a significant portion of our workforce, and many of them are lower-income and have been displaced from the job market in recent years.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While platform workers generally enjoy more flexibility than employees, they are also subject to significant management control by platform companies when their supply of services are matched to demand by algorithms.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Hence, PSP believes that it is timely that our legislation is now being updated to create a new class of workers distinct from employees and self-employed persons to protect the rights of platform workers.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: PSP believes that this is a step in the right direction, which will ensure that younger platform workers have adequate protections for housing and retirement.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: PSP proposes that MOM regularly obtains data points from platform companies to monitor the percentage of jobs completed by platform workers who opt-in to CPF contributions and ensure there is no evidence of platforms discriminating against these workers.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In addition, PSP would like to propose a minimum base fare which could be negotiated between the platform work associations and the platform companies to ensure that platform workers’ income will not be affected by the increase in the operating costs of platform companies.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: On the safety of platform workers, PSP supports the provisions that platform companies must now pay compensation to platform workers for work injuries at the same scope and level as employees are entitled to.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is a much better improvement over the voluntary work injury compensation coverage currently provided out of goodwill by platform companies and will reduce the financial risks and income loss, should a platform worker suffer a work-related injury and unable to work.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: PSP also supports the draft Code of Practice for Platform Services, especially Part 4.5.1, which limits the load to be delivered, because it will better protect platform workers from being exposed to unsafe situations due to excessive loads.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, PSP suggests that Part 4.5.2 of the draft Code of Practice be amended.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Platform workers may feel pressured into accepting jobs during unsafe weather conditions because of the penalties imposed by platform companies on cancellations.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: PSP thus proposes that platform companies remove the penalties for workers who reject or cancel orders during bad weather conditions.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Such cancellations or rejection of orders should not be included when rating the platform worker’s performance.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is taking a leaf from major platform companies, such as Deliveroo, that do not penalise riders in this way.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: PSP calls on the Government to urge platform workers to form platform work associations and work with platform companies to improve working conditions of platform workers, especially in bad weather conditions, to ensure a safe and fair working environment for all platform workers. : Notwithstanding the clarifications and suggestions made in my speech, the PSP supports the Bill.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: These platform operators and platform workers have become an integral part of our society today and in the foreseeable future, with services offered ranging from transport, delivery services and even parcel and logistics management.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: It is, therefore, important that we protect the interests of the platform workers to avoid what some researchers have called “precaritising workers”, leading to the exploitation of labour, unfair treatment of workers, and expanding and enduring inequalities.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: However, governments around the world have found it difficult to confer protection on platform workers, given that they could be classified as independent contractors.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Yet, the platform operators also set the performance markers, the remuneration, the specific jobs and even the routes platform workers are to take by their policies and algorithms.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Platform workers may be penalised if they were to decline work assigned to them by the platform.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This is not unlike an employee in some regards.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Conversely, platform workers bear all the risks of performing the services for the platforms: the risks of accidents, loss of income and even injury on the job to meet the platform’s requirements for service.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: They also bear the cost of the fuel, the rental fees, the insurance premiums and damages to third parties when there are accidents.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: It seems like a lose-lose situation for platform workers because they are considered independent contractors where they are beneficial to the platform operators, but subject to restrictions imposed by the platform operators as though they were employees.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I am, therefore, heartened to see that MOM has worked with various stakeholders and the tripartite partners to come up with this Bill to ensure that the platform workers’ rights are being protected.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: NTUC and the Labour Movement, including myself and my fellow labour Members of Parliament, and Parliamentary colleagues, such as Dr Tan Wu Meng, have been lobbying for changes to protect the rights and interests of freelancers, including platform workers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: In my personal view, this is a landmark and watershed piece of legislation.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: It is a landmark and watershed for three reasons.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This is definitely not an easy endeavour, but we have chosen to take the less trodden path, to do it because it is the right thing to do.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: These are all issues which many unions and jurisdictions are trying to grapple with and many have yet to achieve such a similar breakthrough in terms of scale and impact.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: As raised in this House in 2017, one form of protection is allowing them to have collective representation to ensure their voices are heard.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: While NTUC has created several associations for platform workers to be collectively heard, these associations lack the right to formally represent their members in any disputes with platform operators.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This Bill will allow platform workers to band together collectively to represent their viewpoints, watch for any unfairness and to negotiate with platform operators.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: To provide effective representation, platform work associations under the Bill, need to carry out elections, secret ballots and delegates' conferences on a regular basis, much like how trade unions today are required to do so under the Trade Unions Act.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: However, unlike trade unions, platform work associations will face an uphill task when trying to organise their members and getting them together.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This is due to the nature of the platform workers and the platform work industry being hyper-fluid in nature, where workers can join or leave the platform without necessarily terminating the agreement with the platform operator.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Conversely, platform workers can join new platforms or new platform workers can start doing platform work without too much of a hassle and restrictions in place.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Further, platform workers, by their nature, also work all over Singapore without any fixed workplace.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This hyper-fluidity and de-localised work location create problems not seen in traditional trade unions.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: One issue relates to the conduct of secret ballots and the need for fiscal in-person votes.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: It is relatively straightforward for trade unions to conduct in-person secret ballots given that most workplaces are fixed.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This will enable platform work associations to reach out effectively to their members and facilitate their participation, rather than just a restricted number who manage to come on-site to vote.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
