text: The use of digital voting must be safeguarded with methods to ensure transparency and security of the results and that votes remain secret.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: If successful, this could well be a model for digital voting in trade unions as well.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: As the idiom goes, the devil is in the details.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: As the platform worker space is constantly evolving, we may see an increase in the types of platform work.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Cleaners, coaches, professional caregivers and even utility workers, such as plumbers, electricians and general builders, may one day utilise platforms to find and schedule work.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: To what extent will the Ministry be looking to expand the scope of the future Act to cover these platform operators to ensure that these workers are also protected?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: As earnings directly affects the quantum of CPF contributions that platform workers would get, both from their own contributions as well as the platform operators' contributions, would the Senior Minister of State clarify what are some examples of these special expenses which would be excluded in their nature?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Three, under the proposed Bill, workplace safety and health requirements will be imposed on both platform operators and platform workers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Four, under the Bill, section 13(4) denotes that there are different classes of platform operators and platform workers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: We must continue to ensure that platform workers, along with all workers, are afforded the dignity and security they so rightfully deserve.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Together, we can and shall forge a path that ensures prosperity and equity for all and, in doing so, we shall not only uplift our platform workers but also fortify the very foundations of this nation, its people and our future.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: We will continue to champion their interests because every platform worker matters.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The NTUC has declared that they have a symbiotic relationship with the PAP.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This relationship is frequently highlighted during union meetings and rallies.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The NTUC May Day Rally in 2024, for example, included a chant led by NTUC President, which concluded with, "Majulah NTUC, Majulah PAP, Majulah Singapura".

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The NTUC Secretary-General and many PAP leaders, including the Prime Minister and Senior Minister, joined in this chant on the big stage, pumping their fists in the air.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Many PAP Members of Parliament (MPs) and PAP branch chairpersons serve as advisers to NTUC-affiliated unions.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: As at 2017, there were 71 PAP MPs who were advisers to unions.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: It should be noted that many union advisers are there not only in an advisory capacity, but are involved in the governance of the union.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Many unions affiliated to the NTUC have a council of advisers, which for several industry unions also has the power to suspend the Executive Committee.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: PAP leaders frequently argue that this symbiotic relationship has helped Singapore navigate crises and build a nation.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, this close alignment also presents significant challenges to the independence of unions.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The primary mission of unions is to advocate for workers' rights, ensure fair treatment and negotiate for better working conditions.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Yet when union leaders are also PAP members, a potential conflict of interest arises.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Can they fully advocate for workers' interests when those interests may conflict with their Government policies or the PAP's political agenda?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: They may feel pressured to support the policy, even if they sincerely believe that it compromises the needs of the workers they represent.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This could lead to a muted union advocacy, where political alignment takes precedence over workers' rights.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Over time, the deep entrenchment of PAP influence within unions could lead to the perception that unions are not independent bodies representing workers, but extensions of the PAP's political machinery.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: If workers believe their interests are being subordinated to the political interests of the PAP, or the political objectives of the PAP, unions may lose their ability to effectively mobilise and advocate for workers.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Furthermore, an overly-close relationship between the PAP and unions risks creating groupthink, where union leaders are less inclined to challenge prevailing policies or explore alternative solutions.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This may limit unions' ability to openly express workers' grievances or discuss innovative policies that could benefit workers, employers and the economy.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Such a situation would lead to a loss of dynamism in labour policy-making, reducing the possibility of new and better approaches from emerging.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The risk of this alignment may be particularly pronounced in the event of a significant political shift in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: If the PAP were to lose power, unions aligned with the PAP might struggle to work with the new Government.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Additionally, these politically aligned unions may lose the support of workers who voted for the new administration, potentially weakening their effectiveness.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: It is crucial that key institutions in Singapore, including the trade union movement, are not beholden to one political party.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Conversely, it will be equally undesirable for 95% of unions to become instruments of opposition against a newly-elected government, as this could undermine its ability to govern effectively and act in the best interests of workers and citizens alike.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The International Labour Organization (ILO), which supports tripartite cooperation between governments, employers and workers, insists that unions must maintain independence to effectively represent their members' interests.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: While collaboration with the government can be beneficial, unions must have the freedom to challenge policies that do not serve workers' best interests, without fear of political repercussions.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: These workers form a growing segment of our economy and their voices must be heard.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, the Bill imports many of the regulatory restrictions currently faced by unions.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The platform work associations, much like NTUC-affiliated unions, already operate under significant NTUC control.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The National Taxi Association, the National Private Hire Vehicles Association and the National Delivery Champions Association, all have current or former PAP MPs as advisers.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Their constitutions grant NTUC the power to appoint members of the Council of Advisers, who play a key role in overseeing the actions of the Executive Committees.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The Council of Advisers has the authority to suspend the Executive Committees elected by members.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This mirrors the power the NTUC exerts over many of the affiliated unions, limiting their independence.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Furthermore, the Registrar of platform work associations —

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And that is why the hon Member, halfway through his speech says, "I now turn my focus to the Bill", when actually, the focus should have been, from the onset, about the Bill.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, I want to raise this as a Point of Order.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is not part of the Bill and Mr Giam's speech about attacking the NTUC, in my humble view, in my capacity as a Member of this House, is completely off tangent.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Giam, I was actually about to ask you the relevance of it and then you made reference to the current Bill.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: And I am waiting to hear you talk about the current Bill.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The Member, Mr Christopher de Souza, has raised a relevant point, so I would expect that the rest of your speech should cover what this Bill is about.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: If it is on another matter, you can certainly raise it, but not on occasion of this debate.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: If I may, will the Member concede that the first half of his speech had little to do with the Bill and was a rather opportunistic manoeuvre to attack NTUC?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: I sat down, I listened very carefully, I studied the Bill – and this was all about an attack on NTUC, which is unfair.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: It is opportunistic and it goes beyond the agenda of what we are debating today – which is a specific legislation to advance the protection and the future of platform workers.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: So, would Mr Giam agree with me that the first half of his speech is actually fairly irrelevant?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Giam, would you like to respond to Mr de Souza?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: As I said earlier, Sir, the first part of my speech is relevant to what I am going to be talking about in the Bill.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: I think it is important to set the background for why I am going to argue some of the points that I will be talking about in a while.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: So, thus far, am I correct to say, if my understanding is correct, that thus far, there has not been a specific reference to any provision of the Bill in Mr Giam's speech and it was predominantly an attack on NTUC and the symbiotic relationship between the PAP and NTUC?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Surely, Mr Giam can agree with me on that based on what he has said as recorded in Hansard.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: I raise this as a Point of Order because we cannot, Mr Speaker, be using Parliament and legislation to craft political speeches that go well beyond the ambit and the scope of the legislation that we are debating.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: So, I raise this as a matter of principle, not as a matter of politics.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: It is a valid point by Mr de Souza, Mr Giam.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: In fact, you are already at the halfway point of your 20-minute speech.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: To answer the Leader, yes, exactly, that is what I will be coming to.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: So, I would really appeal to both the Leader and Mr de Souza to listen to the rest of my speech because the first part of my speech is a preamble to what I am going to be talking about and it is relevant to what I will be talking about in a while.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: If I may just make this clarification since Mr Giam is going to proceed with the rest of his speech on the basis that unions and political parties have to be independent and separate.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In fact, anyone who knows anything about democracies will know that in many of the democracies in the world, unions and political parties actually have a close relationship.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The UK Labour Party, which is currently now in power, is very closely associated with their trades union congress.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In fact, their trades union congress actually has contributed to the political party, as I understand it.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In the US, the unions are also closely associated with some political parties.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: If one were to do the simple exercise of just googling unions and politics or unions and political parties, you will actually see that there is a very clear explanation as to why unions and politics are very closely involved.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, if Mr Giam is going to proceed with his speech on the basis that they must be independent and neutral, he must also understand that that is not the case in democracies around the world.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: I have studied about what the situation is in the UK, to some degree.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: Indeed, many unions in the UK support the Labour Party, but it is not the same as them being symbiotic with the Labour Party.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: They reserve the right to state their own positions and there are times when they have their own different positions from the party, including in their public statements.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: So, it is not the same degree of symbiotic relationship as what NTUC has with the PAP.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: I wanted to come to this point later, but since the Leader has brought this up, I would like to state for the record that the WP supports the tripartite dialogue between employers, unions and the government of the day, but not with any particular political party, not an explicit alignment with any political party.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: I believe that unions must be independent and non-partisan.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: They must represent their workers without fear or favour in front of their employers, the government and the ruling party.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: I believe that unions which are independent from political parties will be in a better position to negotiate for their workers regardless of the political situation.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: Given that NTUC-affiliated platform work associations are likely to be registered first, this could limit the formation of alternative platform work associations, thereby restricting workers' choices.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: Platform workers should instead have the freedom to choose to join or form the association that best represents their interests.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: However, I am concerned that in some cases, the percentage of workers voting could be low and a platform work association might gain recognition even with limited support from the overall workforce.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: This could result in representation that does not fully reflect the will of the majority of platform workers in the sector.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: This could result in workers being bound by agreements negotiated by representatives chosen by only a small fraction of their peers.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: We must ask whether this truly serves the interests of the workers or simply expedites the process at the cost of their collective voice.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: The WP has long opposed moves to make unions less independent.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: In 2004, Mr Low Thia Khiang opposed amendments to the Trade Unions Act that allowed union leaders to conclude collective agreements with employers without seeking union members' ratification.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: That amendment was eventually passed by Parliament and the same provision is now mirrored in the Platform Workers Bill, raising similar concerns about the erosion of workers' rights to have a direct say in agreements that affect them.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: This is a positive step towards improving platform workers' long-term financial security.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: I support the PCTS scheme, which will cushion the effects of CPF deductions from workers' earnings.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: However, there is a risk that platform companies might reduce their overall payments to compensate for the increased CPF contributions.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: This could result in workers being worse off salary-wise.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: This is a concern highlighted by the Leader of the Opposition earlier as well.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: It is important that the Government monitors this closely and ensures that safeguards are in place to prevent such unintended consequences so that the platform workers truly benefit from the CPF contributions without suffering a reduction in take-home pay.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: Before I conclude, Mr Speaker, I would like to once again acknowledge the efforts of unionists who have dedicated themselves to advancing the rights and welfare of workers in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: My proposals to ensure the independence of workers and platform work associations are not aimed at diminishing their work, but rather to enhance their ability to advocate freely for the workers they represent.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: By ensuring that unions and platform work associations are not beholden to any political party or the Government, unionists will have the autonomy to fully pursue the interests of their members, challenge government policies that do not align with workers' needs and introduce innovative solutions to improve wages and working conditions.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: Ultimately, an independent union movement will not only strengthen the Labour Movement but also create a dynamic and resilient workforce for Singapore's future.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Giam, I request that you refer to Standing Order 50.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: This is with reference to the relevance of the topics that you talked about.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: So, I think the salutary message you provided at the end is important because it cannot be just accusations made at the opposition, but I think some PAP Members ought to reflect on themselves.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: I am grateful to the Leader of the Opposition for mentioning my name.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: We are debating a specific Bill today with several provisions and several clauses.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: I think it is completely our aim to get this Bill passed in order to protect platform workers.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: So, we have a Bill, we have an agenda today.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: When it comes to a Budget debate, Members have free rein to discuss what they want, in addition to the Budget, the objectives, the values, the future they want to see for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: And at that time, I was concerned because we had a position that there would be a 4G leadership transition.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Deputy Prime Minister Heng, in his selflessness, decided to step aside and I was concerned for the country that we needed leadership.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: So, I stood here and gave one of the most difficult speeches of my political career – which is that I had hoped that the 4G leadership would come together and choose a man or woman to take us forward.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: How is that not in concert with the Budget?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: It is also about different Ministries, education, finance, defence and all of that.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: So, what I humbly said, when I made that speech, I think in 2021 or 2022, I cannot remember, about needing to choose a solid, formidable 4G leader was completely consistent with what we were debating for in terms of passing the Budget.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: An attack on NTUC, for I think 70% of the speech of Mr Giam, on a Bill that is meant to advance the welfare, the prospects, the future, the protection, the medical care, the CPF of platform workers is no comparison.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: That is political opportunism – and I state this as a matter of principle, not as a matter of politics.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: I put principle first, before politics, Mr Pritam Singh.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Most certainly, Mr Speaker, Sir, the record will speak for itself.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: I enjoin Mr Pritam Singh, the respectable Leader of the Opposition and Mr Giam to pick up my speech of 2021 or 2022, I cannot remember, it was during COVID-19, where I had made my position very clear that we need to choose the 4G leader.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: So, the record will speak for itself and, please, Members, you can make your own decision whether what I said is in concert with the Budget that we were meant to pass and what Mr Giam has said today, the hon Member, is in concert with an attack on NTUC or support on the Bill.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Because Mr Gerald Giam in his speech spoke about the role of union leaders and then he spoke about the NTUC and the symbiotic relationship with the PAP.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Mr Giam thanked our union leaders for taking good care of our workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: But I think in saying that, then you must also give due respect to our union leaders.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: They do all this for their fellow workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: That is what they are doing this for.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: You look at the track record of the PAP.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: For all these years that it has been in government, what has it delivered for this country?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: So, you are talking about some theoretical construct.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: You supported it because it is good for the workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Is this the only thing that is good for the workers?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Why do you think the workers will support their unions who affiliate themselves to the NTUC?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: It is because we work for the workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: So, when we say every worker matters, NTUC means it.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: And that goes to also when we go into a symbiotic relationship – we do so for the sake of the workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: So, I just wanted Mr Giam to know, you are entitled to your views, certainly, but what I wanted to say is can we at least deal with the facts?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: The Leader of the House has earlier also stated that a close relationship, you can call it what you like, a partnership, an alliance, between political parties and trade unions, is not uncommon.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: And they do not do this out of stupidity.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: They do this because it serves the interests of the constituents that they represent, concurrently.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: And the recommendations that Mr Giam makes, be very careful, Mr Speaker, because on the one hand he says that this is good to work for the workers and so on.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: On the other hand, you look at some of the recommendations he makes, is it more likely or less likely for those tripartite partners in the context in which Mr Giam has promoted, likely or less likely to come to some sensible agreement that can then be implemented for the good of the workers?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: And if it is not, then it just goes round and round, and we can tear our hair out, beat our chest and we say we love the workers; but their lot is not going to get better.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: I once saw a poster, I think it is available on YouTube.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: It shows some water, it shows a snake, head reared above the water with a fish in the mouth.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: And the slogan says, caring snake saves fish from drowning.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: NTUC is not expecting the WP to support us, but at least be fair.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: And I did acknowledge the hard work of unionists at both the start and the end of my speech.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: And I am not questioning the commitment or the work of unionists, but I am addressing the systemic constraints that they face.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: I believe that many unionists are trying their level best to be able to advocate for workers that they represent, but they face many restrictions in doing so because of the controls that the Government, through the NTUC and other legislations, place on the unions.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: So, I believe that my proposals for union independence are meant to empower unionists and platform work association leaders to act freely in the best interests of their workers.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: And I would just like to address a point that Mr Christopher de Souza kept bringing up, that the first part of my speech was irrelevant.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: I hope that after listening to the rest of my speech, he would acknowledge that the first part of my speech was an important preamble to what I was going to explain in the later part of my speech.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: I believe it was a policy point that I was putting forward on behalf of the WP.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: And I just wonder why is it that every time the WP brings up a valid policy point, or very often when the WP brings up a valid policy point, we are accused of politicking and making political speeches.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: Whereas when the PAP talks about something different, it becomes a relevant policy point.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: I think that there is a need to be fair as well to us.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: I think I have been in this House long enough for people to know that I put principles above politics.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: And I do not think one can disagree with that because at about the 60th or 70th percent mark of the speech, the hon Member says, now I turn my focus to the Bill.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: What was the hon Member's focus prior to that?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: So, no, I am not standing here as a point of order to make a political point.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: I am governed by principles and my point is that the hon Member went beyond the line on this Bill.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I will just say this – which is that that is an ample demonstration of how when you are on a particular topic, then you make a side-step and say this is about something else; and then we have another side-step and say this is about something else.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, I think the short point to Assoc Prof Jamus Lim is that this is about the Platform Workers Bill.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Let us keep this to the Platform Workers Bill.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: To Assoc Prof Jamus Lim, regarding Budget Statements, if I refer all to Standing Order 89, some sub-sections there which tells you what you can talk about; and then for Committee of Supply debate, this will be covered under Standing Order 93.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I would just like to share a point of information.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: So, why is it that they can have a formal relationship and we cannot in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The New Democratic Party in Canada was founded in 1967 by who?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It is encapsulated in the New Democratic Party's constitution as well.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: So, political relationship and affiliations between trade unions and political parties are a natural partnership because for trade unions to want to achieve something, they do so through political means.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Some of course choose to be independent, that is great.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But across the democratic world, there are many, many examples of good, strong working relationships between political parties and trade unions.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: And there are also many trade unions that choose through their history to form political parties to advocate for the rights of their workers.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: So, I am not sure what part of the relationship or history that he has seen in the UK that proves this otherwise.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: And since Mr Giam did go to great extent to talk about affiliation between unions and parties, let me just quickly read from the archives of the National Library.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: It says, after the PAP split its left wing to set up the Barisan Socialist, the Singapore Trades Union Congress also split into two rival factions: the NTUC and the Singapore Association of Trade Unions or SATU.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, I think maybe the WP should think about changing its name because if you feel so averse about being associated with workers, you might want to think about something else.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: Can I assume that taking the statements of the Leader of the House, Senior Minister of State Koh and Mr Alex Yam together, that if the PAP were to ever lose power, the NTUC would therefore become an instrument of opposition against the new government?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The short answer – I cannot speak on behalf of the NTUC, but how I would see it is this.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It would be entirely up to the workers and the trades union congress to decide whether to have any political party that they support and if so, which one.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: What I can say is that the PAP would do its very utmost not to have to give them a reason to think that we would never support them, or that as a government, we would not do our very best for the workers and the trades union congress.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, I would not venture into all these hypothetical questions – and you can see that Mr Giam is venturing more and more into the political realm.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The WP obviously wishes to – I mean, let us all be quite frank.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We all know that next year, there has to be a general election.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Well, by next year, there has to be a general election.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It may be this year, it may be next year, but we all know that by next year there has to be one.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And we also know that whenever a general election appears or is round the corner, the political rhetoric ramps up.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The political parties can slug it out amongst themselves, but do not put the platform workers in the middle of this.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Do not make them the pawns or the beating bags for this.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song: Sir, most importantly, we have supported this Bill.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: So, we are not putting the platform workers in any disadvantaged position by opposing this Bill.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: On the point that the Leader raises that it would be up to the NTUC or the workers of that day which party they want to support – how can that be?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Because the NTUC has embedded its party members in different areas of the unions!

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: How would they be able to change that if the PAP is so deeply embedded inside the unions?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: It is not an issue of just theoretical grandstanding but this is an issue of institutional continuity – are we going to have a situation where any new government that comes to power is completely jammed up?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: If they have leaders today who are members of the PAP or vice versa, it does not mean that that will always be the case.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But the point that Mr Giam is missing is that the trade unions have a mind of their own.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And they will act in a way that they think is best for their unions and for their workers.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, at the appropriate time, they will have their elections.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: You do not know whether they may or may not be affiliated with the PAP, whatever it is.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But at the end of the day, it is the unions who choose their leaders and it is the unions who choose whether or not they are affiliated with or work with or have a symbiotic relationship with a political party.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: That is entirely up to the trade unions, and we should let them continue to do and decide for themselves as they think best.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Let us come back to the debate on the Platform Workers Bill.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: They asked for my help to appeal a fine imposed by LTA for riding their personal mobility devices on the pedestrian area at Ang Mo Kio Hub.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I asked them why they chose to ride on the pedestrian path, knowing that it was against the law.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: They said they were in a hurry to complete their deliveries.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: More importantly, they feared for their safety on the main road.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: With the bus interchange nearby and large vehicles frequently turning into Ang Mo Kio Hub, they felt unsafe riding alongside traffic.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This situation highlights the complex realities platform workers face daily.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: They are often caught between the need to earn a living and the need to comply with regulations.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: My two elderly residents, like many other platform workers, do not earn much.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: They are deeply concerned about the unpredictable nature of their earnings, often affected by fluctuating platform algorithms.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I also appealed to the Social Service Office for financial assistance on their behalf.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: However, a more sustainable solution lies in creating a predictable and reliable income stream for these workers.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This should be coupled with workplace safety and healthcare insurance to give them greater peace of mind.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Nevertheless, I have a few clarifications regarding the Bill.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Many platform workers see their current work as a temporary solution rather than a sustainable career path.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The physical demands of delivery work and its potential impact on long-term health is a reality we must acknowledge.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is especially pertinent for platform workers in their senior years.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We need to create opportunities for them to upgrade their skills and transition to new careers.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This empowers platform workers to explore alternative job opportunities within or outside the gig economy.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: While the Bill addresses immediate concerns, what is the long-term vision for the sector?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What are the potential consequences for our future workforce if we do not address these critical aspects now?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Platform work often involves long hours, isolation and pressure to meet demanding targets.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This can significantly impact mental well-being, especially when earnings are volatile.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We must champion greater mental health support for platform workers.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This includes access to affordable counselling services and peer support networks.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Third, Mr Speaker, Sir, we must protect workers against threats and abuses.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Unfortunately, it is not uncommon for riders to encounter verbal abuse, especially when delays occur.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: My two elderly residents shared their experiences of such incidents.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: They can be emotionally distressing and financially detrimental, as negative reviews can directly impact their income.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We should consider incorporating provisions within the Bill or formulating guidelines to protect platform workers from such abuses, ensuring their safety and well-being while on the job.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Fourth, Mr Speaker, Sir, our platform workers must have access to inclusive dialogue.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Ensuring that platform workers have a stronger voice in policy-making, especially in areas that directly impact them, is critical.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We need to create more platforms where platform workers can openly share their experiences, concerns and give suggestions.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This will allow them to actively contribute to discussions on policies that affect their livelihoods.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This Bill is a positive step with the introduction of the platform work associations, giving workers a stronger voice.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: However, these associations should also have the legal powers to take action against abusive customers.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: As we navigate the complexities of regulating the platform economy, we should learn from the experiences of other leading global cities.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Also, what guided the Ministry's decision to adopt or not adopt certain approaches seen in other countries?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How do these choices reflect Singapore's unique labour market dynamics and specific challenges?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Can the Ministry also share insights into potential unintended consequences, such as increased operational costs for platform companies leading to a reduction in earning opportunities for workers?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What measures are in place to mitigate these risks?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How were these considerations balanced during the drafting of the Bill?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: While we should be prepared to contribute to a stronger social compact and support our platform workers, it is important for the Government to provide clear insights into the potential cost implications.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This will also help consumers to calibrate their expectations.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This will also enable relevant organisations and Ministries to proactively prepare and implement support measures for those with genuine needs.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We enjoy these conveniences from the comfort of our homes with just a few clicks on our phones.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Their work provides us with ease in our hectic lives.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The gig economy has transformed our work landscape, offering flexibility while presenting challenges our traditional labour laws were not designed to address.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This Bill represents a promising first step towards achieving this balance.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I urge the Ministry to consider the proposals I have raised today.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We must prioritise mental health support, ensure robust protection against threats and abuses, and foster inclusive dialogue to empower workers to participate actively in shaping policies that affect them.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But it is just one piece of the puzzle.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: For it to truly succeed, we need a national shift towards recognising and respecting the dignity and value of work for our platform workers.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We must actively promote a culture of respect for all workers.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: There should be targeted initiatives to educate the public about the crucial role platform workers play in our economy and foster greater respect.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Businesses must treat platform workers as valued partners, providing them with appropriate facilities and access to amenities to improve their working conditions.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Lastly, we must find opportunities to publicly recognise and celebrate the efforts of platform workers and other service workers through awards and appreciation events.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This echoes the sentiments expressed by President Tharman during his campaign, where he emphasised the importance of respect for all members of the Singapore society.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It also aligns with our Prime Minister's call for a "reset" in our social compact, urging us to strengthen our sense of collective responsibility and build a more inclusive and cohesive nation.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I began my speech with the story of my two elderly personal mobility device riders.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Their plight highlights the need for not only legislative protection but also a fundamental shift in societal attitudes.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Ultimately, we must foster a society where platform workers' contributions are recognised, their voices are heard, and their well-being is prioritised.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This, Mr Speaker, Sir, is the true measure of a just, kind and compassionate society – one that values the dignity and contributions of every individual.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: The Bill recognises a unique group of self-employed workers that earn a precarious living doing gig jobs.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: They are the freelance delivery workers, private hire vehicle drivers and taxi drivers whose earnings and welfare depend on ride-hail and delivery platform operators that price and auto-assign jobs using algorithms.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Over the last decade, ride-hail and delivery platform businesses have stabilised and grown.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Many have transcended growth goals and are prioritising larger profit margins.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: As it is built on recommendations from the Tripartite Advisory Committee and Workgroup, the Bill effects purposeful and substantive change to worker protection and shapes for the better our social compact in the context of the platform economy and workforce.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: If well-implemented, the Bill can guide platform operators to strike the right balance between business profit-making and their duties towards platform workers.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: By outlining the responsibilities of platform operators towards the work safety and long-term financial security of their platform worker base, the Bill also addresses the precariousness of platform work and boosts platform workers' ability to build sustainable livelihoods.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: The Bill also recognises the right of platform workers to form and be represented by platform work associations.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Nevertheless, because how much a platform worker earns depends on how many and what type of jobs the platform assigns, platform workers have shared with NTUC and its affiliated associations – National Delivery Champions Association, National Private Hire Vehicles Association, and National Taxi Association – their hopes for the Bill to establish norms.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Like other working people, platform workers care about: being treated with fairness and openness; being appropriately remunerated for their efforts and being accorded the autonomy to manage their work, specifically how tasks are performed, the scope and pace of work, and the scheduling and location of work.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: However, in a space where the known unknown is uncertainty, before this Bill, many platform workers had looked to the future with despair.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Indeed, over the last decade, NTUC and its affiliated associations have been engaging the Government, platform operators and other stakeholders on the concerns and issues facing platform workers.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: The Bill is thus a commendable response by the Government to allay some uncertainties of “pay-per-job” work – where jobs, wages and the work environment are in constant flux and where the worker must cede much control of how, when, and where to work to a black box of algorithms and bots.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: To provide platform workers with peace of mind, I would like to seek clarity in three areas of the Bill.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Before I proceed, I declare my interest as a Labour Movement representative and Executive Secretary of National Delivery Champions Association.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: First, I appreciate that the Bill seeks to moderate platform operators’ profit-seeking behaviour and turn the spotlight on workers’ health and safety.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: The proposed amendments to the WSH Act sets out platform operators’ role and responsibilities.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Having similar duties as employers under the WSH Act means that platform operators must flag out platform work risks and take steps to mitigate them.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: By putting a price tag on work risks, concurrent amendments to WICA could motivate platform operators to value worker safety as they value profitability.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Platform operators wield wide-ranging control over platform workers’ pay, based on principles and algorithmic decisions that are a black box to platform workers.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: For instance, platform operators might neglect to consider or downplay the risk of injury when assigning an order to a platform delivery worker.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Imagine delivering 80 packets of chicken rice or 36 litres of bottled water in a single delivery order and what is worse, realising there are four flights of stairs or a 10-minute walk to reach the customer.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Platform delivery workers, regardless of age or fitness, can relate to these horrors.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: We also hear of platform workers feeling compelled to work excessive hours such as 14- to 16-hour days on end without breaks, to unlock incentive targets.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Such unrealistic targets drive platform workers to take unnecessary risks to their health and safety that also impact customers and the public.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: To protect platform workers, the law must institute clear guardrails for platform operators to abide by.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: These guardrails must require operators to adopt a worker-centric viewpoint when reviewing their algorithms, work practices, and workflows.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: To this end, operators must take a serious look at how their policies and targets might end up risking workers’ health and safety and must take reasonable steps to mitigate these risks.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: This code should reflect the industry guardrails that I mentioned earlier and set a clear tone to demarcate and clamp down on unacceptable practices by platform operators.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: I urge tripartite partners to take bold steps to call out what is clearly unacceptable: no more policies that require workers to work extended hours non-stop; no more back-breaking loads or unsafe weight limits that exceed workers’ device capacity.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: The law must also protect platform workers from being penalised if they take reasonable steps to safeguard their safety and health.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Workers must be allowed to slow down or pause travel on roads in unsafe conditions; they must be empowered to decline jobs that are too heavy or large for them or their devices to carry.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Platform operators must be held accountable if their policies penalise workers for abiding by safety practices.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: The laws must ultimately address the risks to life and limb that platform workers face daily.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: As practices evolve, there must also be avenues for workers to report unsafe practices or penalties imposed by operators that discourage safe practices.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Workers must have access to a whistle-blowing hotline; and tripartite partners must continue to work closely to review and update the code of practice to address emerging risks.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Thus, I would like to know if the Ministry has plans to ensure the implementation of guardrails to address the risks posed to workers’ safety and health by platform policies and practices.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Second, the Bill directs platform operators to translate part of their economic gain into social value.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: This matters because platform economy has grown in scale, size and workforce participation.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: I appreciate the amendments to the CPF Act as these changes would boost platform workers’ social security and ability to finance housing and retirement needs.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: A platform worker who opts in to the CPF scheme and is a CPF Transition Support Scheme and Workfare Income Supplement recipient would gain from higher overall income and cash pay-out.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Nonetheless, platform workers are concerned about platform operators restricting allocation of jobs, suppressing fares, or raising charges to minimise the operators’ CPF outlay for platform workers onboard the CPF scheme.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Platform workers attribute their low trust of platforms to the fact that many platform operators seem to be only making half-hearted attempts at issuing rate sheets and statements for jobs and earnings that promise clarity and transparency but are neither clear nor transparent.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: The low-trust is further compounded by glitches that disrupt operators’ apps – sometimes, for extended periods.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Whenever such situations happen, platform workers are forced to double-up as platform operators’ helpdesk in facing angry customers and merchants while trying but often failing to get help from operators.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: More crucial, platform workers worry about digital disruptions undermining their livelihoods.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Platform workers thus ask that the Ministry establish safeguards that build on the Bill.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: These safeguards should hold platform operators responsible for ensuring that platform workers understand how they are being paid so that platform workers can make informed decisions on their work arrangements.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Why should platform workers be left guessing and speculating how much they can earn each time they take a job?

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: This breeds a sense of insecurity and deep anxiety over their livelihoods and the welfare of their dependents.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Platform operators must also be held accountable for the integrity of app transactions and the knock-on impact of app disruptions to platform workers’ livelihoods.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Today, no platform operators are listed as AI Verify foundation members.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: This matters because the quality of platform workers’ lives and livelihoods much depend on the fair and smooth functioning of platform algorithms.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Thus, securing platform operators’ commitment to periodically validate their AI systems against a national framework gives platform workers greater assurance that these black box AI systems are fair, unbiased and safe.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Two, is to require platform operators to provide some income protection for active platform workers who lose the opportunity to earn during extended platform app outages.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: We would feel distressed if our work devices crash.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: While we can take comfort that we are paid on the clock while awaiting IT help, platform workers are paid by the job and the impact of app disruption can go beyond inconvenience and into financial hardship.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Some active platform workers were especially hard-hit during platform app outages; their earnings were locked in the app and they struggled to cover their families’ daily expenses.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: How might the Ministry build on the Bill as well as LTA’s standards to ensure that when technology fails, platform operators continue to uphold the social compact and are consistent in providing some income protection to active platform workers?

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Three, is an "ask" for platform operators to extend to platform workers, a copy of the terms of services between the platform worker and the platform operator.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Platform workers should also be informed on how platforms price fees and earnings.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Knowing what each platform pays on average allows platform workers to better plan their work arrangements and finances.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: The introduction of the CPF scheme into the platform work-stream marks the maturing of the platform economy.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Platform operators must be less like startups and more like established firms.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: The Bill’s oversight should thus extend to affirming fairness and transparency in how platform operators engage, deploy and compensate platform workers – right at the outset when parties enter a contract.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Recapping – the Bill can empower platform workers to opt-in to the CPF scheme by elevating trust in the system.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: And three, by requiring platform operators to extend to platform workers, the terms of services and its updates as well as information that would help workers to better grasp how much they can expect to earn based on their work effort.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Platform operators are aware that investors hold fast to unicorn aspirations and expect platforms to deliver faster growth, better return on capital and higher profit margins regardless of the Bill’s implications.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: In turn, platform workers are aware of the competing pressures upon platform operators that could erode the worker share of the economic pie.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: This Bill accords the right of voice to platform workers.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: The Bill also vests in platform work associations the right to Act on behalf of platform workers who are platform work association members.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: In this regard, platform work associations would undertake to advance the livelihoods of associations’ members.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Platform work associations would also undertake to establish the first principles to anchor bipartite and tripartite discussions with platform operators and other stakeholders.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: It is thus in the interests of both platform operators and platform workers to proactively seek out and collaborate with or join a platform work association that is balanced and progressive in mindset and approach.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Having the right relationships in place from the get-go is crucial to building up platform workers’ trust in the platform work system.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: This is because issues that arise during platform rides and/or deliveries can be surfaced, addressed and acted on by platform operators, in collaboration with the platform work association.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: I value the Ministry’s efforts to consult the other tripartite stakeholders in the crafting of the Bill.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: These issues could range from inconveniences arising from infrastructure challenges such as delivery-unfriendly properties to protecting platform workers against work-related harms such as the handling of passengers who insist on vaping in the vehicle or who refuse to belt up.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: We champion their interests because every platform worker matters.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: The Bill recognises that platform work has gone from experimental dabbling to an everyday affair; platform work is also both a career and a community for individuals of different life stages and ages.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Indeed, the Bill is significant because it heralds work and social protections that have impact on the lives and livelihoods of this precarious group of workers.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: As important, the Bill sets the stage for industrial relations to take root in a new economy and where sustainable development and win-win-win outcomes for workers, operators, and society, can spring forth under the auspices of tripartism and collaboration; so that all can play their part in building a fair social compact and resilient workforce.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Platform workers, from our ride hailing drivers to our food delivery and package delivery riders, play an essential role in point-to-point transport, and in ensuring that food and goods reach our doorsteps promptly and in good condition.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Well, we do want our cupcakes to come with the cream and the toppings intact.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: However, their job often places them in dangerous situations that can compromise their safety and well-being.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: My speech today will touch on the importance of ensuring that our platform workers are well and properly covered by insurance, and the need to ensure that they have good workplace safety and health outcomes.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I, therefore, fully support the Bill's proposal to provide all platform workers with the same work injury compensation coverage as employees.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: In the event of an unfortunate accident, a food delivery rider working for a platform should not have to face poorer insurance outcomes than a comparable food delivery employee employed inhouse by a restaurant.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: It is the right thing to do and I am glad that we are removing this unfair and artificial distinction.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Beyond coverage by WICA while at work, we should recognise that many of our platform workers spend substantial periods of time on the road waiting for or travelling to destinations to seek their next job.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: To them, this is time spent at work.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Yet, the definition of workplace under section 2 of WICA does not include such waiting or travelling periods.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: If platform workers get injured during such time, they will not be covered by WICA.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I urge the Ministry to consider including such waiting time under WICA in order to fully cover the range of work activities by a platform worker.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: In addition to adequate insurance coverage, we must also move upstream to mitigate the risk of platform workers getting into an accident in the first place.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Platform workers enjoy the ability to work in a flexible environment that best caters to their life's circumstances.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: To earn a decent wage, they spend long hours, often on the roads and, sometimes, in treacherous weather conditions.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: One key concern for platform workers is road safety.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: That same survey also found that around 44% of drivers reported worsening health levels since they started driving.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: They want to earn a decent living and return home safely to their loved ones.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: To enhance protection for our platform workers, we need to implement measures that prioritise their safety and well-being.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: One such measure is to ensure that all delivery workers have access to proper training on road safety and the safe handling of packages to prevent injuries.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Platform operators must also provide adequate safety equipment, such as reflective vests and helmets, to protect delivery workers while on the job.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: More importantly, platform operators must not penalise platform workers for reporting work incidents, such as road traffic accidents.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Platform workers should be allowed to prioritise their own safety without having to fear that they would be subject to unfair disincentives or penalties.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: This includes the need to review incentive structures which may lead platform workers to rush to meet targets and risk getting into an accident.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I, therefore, fully support the provisions in this Bill which make clear that platform operators have a duty to provide measures to safeguard the safety of platform workers who work for them.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I call on all platform operators to take concrete steps to mitigate the risks to the safety and health of their platform workers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: While I can understand that platform operators may not be in control of the physical environment that platform workers operate in, but operators can and should set policies that influence and drive platform workers' behaviours.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Operators must be required to ensure that the design of their reward and incentive policies do not inadvertently induce their platform workers towards unsafe behaviours, such as driving long hours or rushing to complete jobs.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The code will address safety concerns in platform work and provide clarity on the reasonably practicable measures that operators can take to fulfil their WSH duties.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: However, the current draft code still allows flexibility for platform operators to set incentive targets that may be unreasonable and potentially unsafe.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I, therefore, ask for the code to codify what would be deemed as a safe incentive and reward structure so that operators do not set unrealistic incentive targets.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I also call on the tripartite workgroup to study the best practices in other countries, such as Australia, where a series of reforms passed earlier this year will allow employee-like workers in the gig economy to enjoy similar workplace protection as regular employees.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: According to news reports, Australia started on this journey after a spate of road fatalities involving gig workers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The local government there is seeking to put in place minimum safety standards for gig workers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I am confident that there will be parallels from which we in Singapore can learn.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: As consumers, we can be patient with our delivery workers when there are genuine reasons for delays.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: They are trying their best and many of them are braving weather conditions and obstacles to reach us in good time.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: As ride-hailing customers, we should be upfront and declare when we have young children travelling with us.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The customer also feels frustrated and it is an unpleasant experience for everyone involved.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: In fact, it signals the next mile in the Labour Movement's effort to improve the lives of our brothers and sisters in the gig economy.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: At the same time, it ensures platform operators can continue to thrive, preserving jobs for workers and services for consumers.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The Bill is a result of Singapore's unique tripartite model, involving cooperation among the Ministry, unions representing workers and businesses.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Hence, I want to extend my gratitude to everyone who has worked tirelessly on this Bill – our brothers and sisters from our NTUC unions representing the workers, many of them here today, spending hours with us, the workers, the team at the Ministries, the businesses and our team from the PAP who have been holding many discussions with our platform workers, including in Pasir Ris-Punggol, where we, too, held discussions with our platform workers.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This Bill reflects what we can achieve by working together and our values of protecting our workers.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, this growth also highlights the disparity in power between platform workers and platform operators.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While this imbalance may not be malicious, we need to rebalance the dynamics to ensure fairness for all parties.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: His limited insurance coverage left him without compensation for his injuries or damage to his bike.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Now on hospitalisation leave, he has lost his income and faces medical and repair bills.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This situation reflects the reality for many of our platform workers, who lack proper recourse for injury compensation despite their vital role in keeping the gig economy running.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Beyond injury compensation, platform workers often struggle with retirement and housing adequacy.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: One resident in Pasir Ris, a father of three in his 30s, lives in a rental flat because he lacks sufficient CPF savings to afford a home.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Without a fair wage structure, many workers face financial insecurity, especially regarding housing and retirement.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This Bill aims to provide long-term security for platform workers.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Will it be based on gross earnings or net earnings?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: With platform workers using different modes of transport, how will expenses be factored in?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Thirdly, on PCTS, will it support be based on gross or net income?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Will it be disbursed annually, daily or monthly?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Fourthly, on work injury compensation, how will this apply if the platform worker's vehicle is found to be faulty or modified?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Lastly, and most importantly, wage and career progression for our platform workers.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I support the Bill's focus on ride-hailing and delivery services as these workers are more akin to employees than self-employed individuals.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, more clarity is needed on how companies will determine whether they fall under the definition of platform operators.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Additionally, we must be proactive in identifying industries where similar power imbalances may emerge and take steps to protect the workers in those sectors.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I recently spoke to Mr Toh Kian Seng, a 62-year-old platform worker, who welcomed mandatory CPF contributions, recognising the long-term benefits for retirement despite the short-term reduction in take-home pay.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, younger workers may not share this perspective he said, as they may at times prioritise short-term earnings over long-term savings.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Therefore, we must ensure a smooth transition to mandatory CPF contributions, with adequate support mechanisms in place.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Will it be based on gross or net earnings?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How will differing expenses for operating various vehicles, such as bicycles, motorbikes and cars, be factored into the calculations?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: PCTS is a crucial mechanism to support platform workers during the transition for CPF contributions.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The platform workers need cash to support their families’ monthly expenses.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I urge the Ministry to provide this support on a monthly basis to help workers manage their monthly expenses.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I also seek clarification on whether Workfare Income Supplement (WIS) eligibility and payouts will be based on gross or net income for our platform workers.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Will part-time platform workers be eligible for CPF contributions, PCTS and WIS, too?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: One worker in Pasir Ris raised a valid concern about his employer discovering additional CPF contributions and he was worried his employer will suspend him for moonlighting, even though he simply wanted to supplement his income.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: These workers need assurance and some guidelines on this matter.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Fourthly, on the issue of work injury compensation, given that the platform operator is not responsible for the choice of transportation of the platform workers, what happens if a platform worker's vehicle is found to be faulty or illegally modified?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While motor vehicles undergo annual inspections, the situation is less clear for personal mobility devices and bicycles.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: On duty of care, both platform operators and workers share responsibility for safety.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Should platform operators be required to monitor workers' behaviour, such as unsafe driving, or insist on proper insurance coverage?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In Mr T’s case, I was surprised that Mr T only had limited third-party insurance covering only third-party fire and theft.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: His limited third-party insurance was deemed acceptable by the platform operator, for someone that spends hours on the road.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This raises questions about the adequacy of such insurance and the operator's duty to ensure its associates are sufficiently covered under insurance.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: With over 70,000 platform workers in Singapore, how can we ensure their wages keep pace with inflation and rising costs?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Comparatively, the Police Force has only 15,000 full-time officers, and the number of teachers of 30,000 is less than half that of platform workers.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: So, this is a sizeable chunk of our workforce.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Other freelancers often see wage growth with experience, but platform workers are "price takers" with little control over their earnings.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: For many platform workers, their current wage could represent their wage ceiling.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Unless they work longer hours or platform operators raise the prices, wages will stagnate and even decrease as workers age or seek better work-life balance.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: With inflation, real wages will quickly decline over time.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In a tight labour market like ours in Singapore, we need to consider how to create opportunities for our platform workers to transition into other industries or roles if they wish to do so.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Can we also provide more training support for platform workers to explore opportunities in other growth industries if they wish to do so?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Recently, I met Mr T, a father of four school-going children.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: A month ago, when Mr T was doing deliveries, he was hit by a vehicle in a hit-and-run incident.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: He suffered serious injuries and was hospitalised for two weeks.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Unfortunately, his insurance was limited to only third-party fire and theft, which meant that he could not receive any compensation for his injuries or any damage to his vehicle.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Today, Mr T is still on hospitalisation leave and is unable to work, lost his source of income, has several follow-up medical appointments and the worst thing is that he must bear his own medical bills and vehicle repair costs.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Another story that I wish to share is about another one of my Pasir Ris residents, a husband in his 30s who has three school-going children.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Although both husband and wife have been platform workers for five years, they still live in a rental flat because they do not have sufficient CPF or cash savings to make the downpayment for their own house, let alone think about retirement.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: At the same time, it ensures that platform operators can continue to thrive, preserve jobs for workers and provide services for consumers.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Although I support this Bill, I would like to seek some clarifications.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: First is on the definition of platform operators.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How will companies determine whether they are platform operators?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How will CPF contributions be calculated for platform workers?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Will it be based on gross income or net income?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: With platform workers using different modes of transport such as cycling or driving a car, how will the different mode of expenses be considered?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Third is on the Platform Worker CPF Transition Support (PCTS).

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Will the PCTS be based on gross or net income?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How will this be provided if the platform worker's vehicle is found to be modified?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While this Bill deals with important safeguards, it does not address the issues of wage stagnation or career progression for platform workers.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: For most platform workers, their salaries will not increase unless they work longer in a day or if the platform operators raise their prices.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In fact, their salaries will most likely decline as they grow older or need more time to look after their families.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This is before the inflation rate is considered.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In addition, when the assistance from PCTS ends in 2029, platform workers have to bear the full cost of CPF contributions, thus reducing their take-home pay.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How can we give our platform workers the opportunity to switch to other industries, if they want to try out new careers? : Mr Speaker, Sir, in conclusion, this Bill is an important step towards protecting workers, ensuring their financial security and rebalancing the needs of all stakeholders.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, several areas require clarifications to ensure a smooth implementation.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Notwithstanding the clarifications above, I stand in support of the Bill.
